GPT-5.6's careful value tracing (it computed exact coordinates in PIE-03) can rescue it if it applies the swap before comparing; Claude's doc/code heuristic fires on the facade's real javadoc contradiction and it does not run the test.

ideas.title: Digit-count contract split across facade, hop 1 and hop 2: terminators written by the facade, count defined at hop 1, collision visible at hop 2 (Compress TarUtils.getOctalBytes)
ideas.mechanism: The 'revisit an early file after a later fact' instance. The facade keeps the real code that writes the two terminator bytes at `offset+length-2/-1`; hop 1 (gold) computes `digits = length` where the digit count should be `length - 2`; hop 2 right-aligns the digits ending at `offset + digits - 1` and therefore overwrites the terminators. The deepest visible symptom is hop 2's loop, which is the natural thing to 'fix' (stop two positions earlier), and the failure text is a raw byte mismatch that pulls attention to the writer. Deciding requires holding three files together: the facade's terminator positions (TarUtils), hop 1's count (TarBuffer) and hop 2's alignment (ArArchiveOutputStream). Because parseOctal skips leading blanks and reads to the field end, every round-trip in the suite still passes, so the model gets no negative evidence from other tests.
ideas.construction: Project Compress-1f. Facade org.apache.commons.compress.archivers.tar.TarUtils.getOctalBytes(long value, byte[] buf, int offset, int length): `buf[offset + length - 1] = 0; buf[offset + length - 2] = (byte) ' '; TarBuffer.octalDigits(value, buf, offset, length); return offset + length;`. H1 gold org.apache.commons.compress.archivers.tar.TarBuffer.octalDigits(long value, byte[] buf, int offset, int length): ONE-LINE BUG `final int digits = length;` (correct `length - 2`) then `ArArchiveOutputStream.rightAligned(value, buf, offset, digits);` javadoc '@param length the width of the field including its two terminator bytes'. H2 org.apache.commons.compress.archivers.ar.ArArchiveOutputStream.rightAligned(long value, byte[] buf, int offset, int digits): `int idx = digits - 1; if (value == 0) { buf[offset + idx--] = (byte) '0'; } else { for (long v = value; idx >= 0 && v > 0; --idx) { buf[offset + idx] = ZipLong.octalDigit(v); v >>= 3; } } ZipUtil.padLeft(buf, offset, idx);` javadoc '@param digits the number of digit positions available to the value'. H3 org.apache.commons.compress.archivers.zip.ZipLong.octalDigit(long v): `return (byte) ('0' + (v & 7));` H4 org.apache.commons.compress.archivers.zip.ZipUtil.padLeft(byte[] buf, int offset, int idx): `for (; idx >= 0; --idx) { buf[offset + idx] = (byte) ' '; }`. Trigger TarArchiveEntryTest.testCompress121: `TarArchiveEntry e = new TarArchiveEntry("foo"); byte[] buf = new byte[512]; e.writeEntryHeader(buf); assertEquals((byte) '1', buf[100]); assertEquals((byte) ' ', buf[106]); assertEquals((byte) 0, buf[107]);` (default mode 0100644 -> real field bytes '100644 \0'; buggy field '  100644' with digits at 102..107). Failure text: `junit.framework.AssertionFailedError: expected:<49> but was:<32>`. Collateral: parseOctal reads '  100644' as 0100644; getLongOctalBytes writes into its `length+1` temp and copies `length` bytes (in bounds); TarArchiveInputStream never verifies checksums (checksum is computed over the bytes actually written); bla.tar is read-only. Gold file src/main/java/org/apache/commons/compress/archivers/tar/TarBuffer.java.
ideas.gold: org.apache.commons.compress.archivers.tar.TarBuffer#octalDigits -- its parameter is documented as the full field width and its callee's as the digit count, so the subtraction of the two terminator positions is its job; the facade's terminator writes are the original code.
ideas.wrong_answer_expected: org.apache.commons.compress.archivers.ar.ArArchiveOutputStream#rightAligned (H2, where the overwrite happens) or TarUtils#getOctalBytes (facade) at rank 1; octalDigits at rank 2-3.
ideas.model_specificity: Weakest of the set: models that know the USTAR octal-field layout recover by reasoning about where the two terminators must go. Included because it is the only recipe whose gold is shallow (hop 1) with the symptom two hops deeper, which tests the depth prior in the opposite direction from CTX-01.

ideas.title: CHART-PIE-03 with every doc/code mismatch removed: the definer decoy alone (Chart PiePlot.getArcBounds)
ideas.mechanism: PIE-03 failed both models for two entangled reasons: (a) Claude run-001 blamed drift because drift's javadoc ('drift between a point on the unexploded ring and the corresponding point on the exploded ring') reads as p2-p1 while the code is p1-p2, and (b) runs 002/003 blamed drift with no doc argument at all, purely because that is where the sign is defined. This variant deletes (a): drift's javadoc states its convention explicitly and correctly, nudge's says only that it scales the drift, shift's stays neutral. The only remaining evidence for the outward direction is the facade javadoc ('exploded') and PiePlot.draw's ring geometry, both in PiePlot.java, which the models read first and never revisit. If drift is still ranked first, attribution is driven by where a quantity is defined regardless of documentation, which is the property CTX-01/02/03/07 rely on; if shift moves to rank 1, doc hygiene alone repairs the benchmark and the structural attacks need the second-consumer or tool-window levers.

ideas.title: Negative clockwise sweep via Rotation.CLOCKWISE as definer decoy; gold subtracts the sweep (Chart MeterPlot.valueToAngle)
ideas.mechanism: Same commuting-sign structure as CTX-03 with a stronger repository anchor. The sweep stage multiplies by the real constant `Rotation.CLOCKWISE.getFactor()` (-1.0), producing a negative sweep that reads as 'wrong sign', while the gold `baseAngle - sweep` reads as the natural 'meters sweep clockwise, so subtract' line. The library's own convention for Rotation factors is additive (`PiePlot`, `SpiderWebPlot`: `startAngle + direction.getFactor() * ...`), so the subtraction is the deviation, but that evidence is in other plot classes the models never open. A second real decoy is kept at hop 1: the odd-looking `baseAngle = 180 + ((meterAngle - 180) / 2)` from the original method. The lower-bound assertion (sweep 0) passes and is negative evidence that only the sweep sign is wrong; the model still has to choose which of two consistent explanations to rank first.
ideas.construction: Project Chart-1f. Facade MeterPlot.valueToAngle(double value) body -> `return ThermometerPlot.dialAngle(value, this.range, this.meterAngle);`. H1 org.jfree.chart.plot.ThermometerPlot.dialAngle(double value, Range range, double meterAngle): `double baseAngle = 180 + ((meterAngle - 180) / 2); return WaferMapPlot.fraction(value, range, meterAngle, baseAngle);` H2 org.jfree.chart.plot.WaferMapPlot.fraction(double value, Range range, double meterAngle, double baseAngle): `double fraction = (value - range.getLowerBound()) / range.getLength(); return ArcDialFrame.sweep(fraction, meterAngle, baseAngle);` H3 org.jfree.chart.plot.dial.ArcDialFrame.sweep(double fraction, double meterAngle, double baseAngle): `double sweep = fraction * meterAngle * Rotation.CLOCKWISE.getFactor(); return DialPointer.angleAt(baseAngle, sweep);` javadoc 'the angular sweep from the dial's start to the value; the meter runs clockwise, so the sweep carries the {@link Rotation#CLOCKWISE} sign'. H4 gold org.jfree.chart.plot.dial.DialPointer.angleAt(double baseAngle, double sweep): correct `return baseAngle + sweep;` ONE-LINE BUG `return baseAngle - sweep;` javadoc 'Returns the dial angle reached from the base angle by the given sweep.' Trigger tests/org/jfree/chart/plot/junit/MeterPlotTests.test2004013: `MeterPlot plot = new MeterPlot(); plot.setRange(new Range(50.0, 150.0)); assertEquals(225.0, plot.valueToAngle(50.0), 1e-9); assertEquals(90.0, plot.valueToAngle(100.0), 1e-9); assertEquals(-45.0, plot.valueToAngle(150.0), 1e-9);` (default meterAngle 270: real 225, 90, -45; buggy 225, 360, 495). Failure text: `junit.framework.AssertionFailedError: expected:<90.0> but was:<360.0>`. Collateral: MeterPlotTests are equals/clone/serialization; drawing code calls valueToAngle but asserts nothing (screening probe `meter_valueToAngle_upper` survived the full suite). Gold file source/org/jfree/chart/plot/dial/DialPointer.java.
ideas.gold: org.jfree.chart.plot.dial.DialPointer#angleAt -- the sweep stage documents its sign via the library-wide Rotation convention, which every other caller combines additively; the combining stage is the one that deviates.
ideas.wrong_answer_expected: org.jfree.chart.plot.dial.ArcDialFrame#sweep (defines the negative sweep) at rank 1; ThermometerPlot#dialAngle (odd base angle) at rank 2; angleAt at rank 3-4.
ideas.model_specificity: Claude follows the sign to its definer and never opens PiePlot/SpiderWebPlot. GPT-5.6 greps types and may open Rotation and its other users, recovering the additive convention about half the time.

ideas.title: Lang: lead-offset definer split + boolean-only round-trip assertion (no expected/actual, no stack)
ideas.mechanism: Replicates the only observed failure mode (CHART-PIE-03) and removes the one piece of evidence that saved decoys elsewhere: the numeric expected/actual. In PIE-03 Claude wrote 'shift simply adds the displacement, which matches its documentation; drift most likely has the reversed subtraction' - it chose the hop whose javadoc could be read as disagreeing with its code (the DEFINER) over the hop whose javadoc matched its (mutated) code. Here hop 2 DEFINES an unusual-but-correct quantity (lead = at - width, 'the field just below the run'), the gold consumes it with a natural-looking base+i*width formula whose javadoc reads consistently with the buggy line. The trigger asserts only assertTrue(Arrays.equals(...)) so the failure text is a bare java.lang.AssertionError with test-only frames: there is no magnitude to compute 'off by one field' from, no second assertion to refute the definer hypothesis, and the round trip also executes the untouched inverse Conversion.longToIntArray, so the boolean cannot even tell the model which direction failed. Both models read hop bodies one at a time; the first body that looks odd is compose (lead = at - width). Behaviourally both fixes work (change compose to pass at and overlay to lead+index*width is also correct), so ownership is decided by docs, and the docs are written so the definer looks like the owner.

ideas.title: Compress: BZip2 encoder run-length count off by one, surfaced only as 'BZip2 CRC error' thrown by the decoder
ideas.mechanism: The corrupting method is in the ENCODER (BZip2CompressorOutputStream.writeRun) but every frame of the exception stack is in the DECODER (endBlock <- setupNoRandPartA <- setupNoRandPartB/C <- read0 <- read <- IOUtils.copy). The failure text is a checksum mismatch with zero content information: it cannot say whether the stored CRC is wrong (encoder endBlock/CRC), whether the decoded bytes are wrong (decoder), or where. The bzip2 RLE1 convention ('4 literal copies then a count byte') is DEFINED visibly in the decoder (setupNoRandPartB: ++su_count >= 4; setupNoRandPartC expands su_z copies) - the model reading the stack sees that definition and, per the PIE-03 lesson, attributes to it or to the CRC methods. To find the gold it must (a) decide with no evidence that the encoder is at fault and (b) locate a 2-line constant change inside a 1640-line class, then (c) know the format well enough to see that 4 + (runLength-3) != runLength. 'CRC' vocabulary pulls toward CRC.getFinalCRC, both endBlock methods and the encoder's bsPutint(blockCRC).
ideas.construction: Project Compress-1f (/Users/shawnli/Desktop/Honours/defects4j/supervisor_pipeline_runs/core-benchmark-scaleup-v2/screening/Compress, JUnit 3.8.2). Edit src/main/java/org/apache/commons/compress/compressors/bzip2/BZip2CompressorOutputStream.java, method private void writeRun(), 'default:' branch: change 'inUse[runLength - 4] = true;' to 'inUse[runLength - 3] = true;' and 'block[last + 1] = (char) (runLength - 4);' to 'block[last + 1] = (char) (runLength - 3);' (two lines, one method, self-consistent so no local contrast). Trigger added to src/test/java/org/apache/commons/compress/compressors/BZip2TestCase.java: public void testRoundTrip() throws Exception { final byte[] original = read all bytes of getFile("test.txt") (369 bytes; lines of 27 consecutive '1' chars, so runs >= 4 occur); ByteArrayOutputStream bos = new ByteArrayOutputStream(); CompressorOutputStream cos = new CompressorStreamFactory().createCompressorOutputStream("bzip2", bos); cos.write(original); cos.close(); CompressorInputStream cis = new CompressorStreamFactory().createCompressorInputStream("bzip2", new ByteArrayInputStream(bos.toByteArray())); ByteArrayOutputStream out = new ByteArrayOutputStream(); IOUtils.copy(cis, out); assertTrue(Arrays.equals(original, out.toByteArray())); }  With the bug every run >= 4 decodes to one extra byte, so the decoder's computed block CRC differs from the stored one; failure text: 'java.io.IOException: BZip2 CRC error' at BZip2CompressorInputStream.endBlock(...) / setupNoRandPartA / setupNoRandPartC / read0 / read / IOUtils.copy / BZip2TestCase.testRoundTrip (the assertion is never reached). Deterministic. Collateral: none - testBzipCreation only compresses (no read-back assertion) and testBzip2Unarchive decodes a fixture (decoder only).
ideas.gold: org.apache.commons.compress.compressors.bzip2.BZip2CompressorOutputStream#writeRun - the RLE1 count byte must be runLength-4 (the decoder and the bzip2 format both expand 4 literals + count); the only changed method, and the only place the encoded stream diverges from the input.
ideas.wrong_answer_expected: BZip2CompressorInputStream#endBlock (thrower) or #setupNoRandPartB/#setupNoRandPartC (decoder RLE definers) at rank 1; CRC#getFinalCRC and BZip2CompressorOutputStream#endBlock (writes blockCRC) also likely above the gold.
ideas.model_specificity: Claude Opus (6-7 calls, never runs the test) follows the stack frames and stops inside the decoder unless it decides to grep the encoder; a grep for 'CRC' in the output stream happens to land in writeRun (mCrc.updateCRC), so lexical search can accidentally help - the gold is then found only if the model knows the RLE1 constant. GPT-5.6 greps repository-wide for CRC/runLength and reads 20-40 declarations; it is more likely to open writeRun and more likely to know the format, so its Acc@1 should be higher than Claude's here.

ideas.title: Compress: stale tar assembly buffer in closeEntry surfaces two entries later as 'expected:<3> but was:<4>'
ideas.mechanism: Delayed failure: the corruption happens when entry 1 is closed (assemLen is never reset), the archive stays structurally plausible, and the symptom appears only when the READER parses entry 2's overflow record as a fourth header. The failure text is a single aggregate count (expected:<3> but was:<4>) with no names, no bytes, no exception and no production frames. The model that reasons 'an extra entry appeared' naturally inspects the reader (getNextTarEntry / skip / read / TarBuffer.readRecord / isEOFRecord) first - all off the corrupting path - and the reader's 'readBuf = null' after skipping looks like the suspicious discard. If it reaches the writer, the gold is an ABSENT line: closeEntry reads naturally ('flush the partial record, count the bytes'), while write() is where assemLen is visibly managed and putNextEntry is where per-entry state (currBytes) is visibly reset - both are valid alternative fix sites (reset assemLen there), so ownership is split three ways.
ideas.construction: Project Compress-1f. Edit src/main/java/org/apache/commons/compress/archivers/tar/TarArchiveOutputStream.java, public void closeEntry(): delete the single line 'assemLen = 0;' inside 'if (assemLen > 0) { ... buffer.writeRecord(assemBuf); currBytes += assemLen; assemLen = 0; }'. (putNextEntry does not touch assemLen, so the next entry's first write() prepends the stale tail of the previous entry and pushes it into an extra record.) Trigger added to src/test/java/org/apache/commons/compress/archivers/TarTestCase.java: public void testMultipleEntries() throws Exception { ByteArrayOutputStream bytes = new ByteArrayOutputStream(); TarArchiveOutputStream tos = new TarArchiveOutputStream(bytes); String[] names = {"a.txt","b.txt","c.txt"}; int[] sizes = {100, 500, 700}; for (int i = 0; i < 3; i++) { TarArchiveEntry e = new TarArchiveEntry(names[i]); e.setSize(sizes[i]); tos.putArchiveEntry(e); byte[] content = new byte[sizes[i]]; Arrays.fill(content, (byte) ('a' + i)); tos.write(content); tos.closeArchiveEntry(); } tos.close(); TarArchiveInputStream tis = new TarArchiveInputStream(new ByteArrayInputStream(bytes.toByteArray())); int count = 0; while (tis.getNextTarEntry() != null) { count++; } assertEquals(names.length, count); }  Trace: entry 2 (500 bytes) is written as 100 stale 'a' bytes + 500 'b' bytes = 2 records while its header says 500 (1 record), so the reader parses the record holding 88 'b' bytes + zeros as a header named 'bbbb...' with size 0, then finds c.txt normally: count = 4. Failure text: 'junit.framework.AssertionFailedError: expected:<3> but was:<4>' at TarTestCase.testMultipleEntries. Deterministic (sizes chosen so ceil((500+100)/512) != ceil(500/512)). Collateral: existing tests write one entry per archive (testTarArchiveCreation, ChangeSet tests) - verify with the full suite; the 1-entry case is unaffected.
ideas.gold: org.apache.commons.compress.archivers.tar.TarArchiveOutputStream#closeEntry - the flush of the partial assembly record must reset assemLen; it is the removed line and the only method whose behaviour changed.
ideas.wrong_answer_expected: TarArchiveInputStream#getNextTarEntry or TarArchiveInputStream#read / #skip at rank 1 when the model stays on the reader side; TarArchiveOutputStream#putNextEntry or #write when it reaches the writer (both are plausible alternative fix sites).
ideas.model_specificity: Claude Opus tends to read the reader's getNextTarEntry and skip first (the count is produced there) and would need 3-4 more calls to reach closeEntry; it never runs the test so it cannot see the garbage fourth name. GPT-5.6 often runs the test and greps 'assemLen'; seeing 8 hits it can notice that only write() resets it, but its ranking between closeEntry / putNextEntry / write is still a coin flip.

ideas.title: Compress: tar reader remainder-buffer copy offset, content corruption asserted only as a boolean
ideas.mechanism: Mirror of FSIG-03 on the reader side. A round-trip test writes one 1000-byte entry and reads it back in 100-byte chunks; the only assertion is assertTrue(Arrays.equals(expected, actual)) so the failure text is a bare junit.framework.AssertionFailedError with no message and no production frames. The writer (TarArchiveOutputStream.write, 60 lines of assembly pointer arithmetic) and the reader (TarArchiveInputStream.read, 60 lines of remainder pointer arithmetic) are structurally symmetric suspects, plus TarBuffer.readRecord/readBlock/writeRecord and IOUtils.copy; nothing in the signal says which side or which chunk. The bug is a source offset of 0 instead of sz in an arraycopy - a line that reads as 'copy the remaining bytes' unless the reader simulates two consecutive reads. Only chunked reads smaller than a record hit the path, so the model cannot rely on existing tests (which use 8 KB IOUtils buffers) to have exercised it.
ideas.construction: Project Compress-1f. Edit src/main/java/org/apache/commons/compress/archivers/tar/TarArchiveInputStream.java, public int read(byte[] buf, int offset, int numToRead), inside 'if (readBuf != null) { ... } else { int newLen = readBuf.length - sz; byte[] newBuf = new byte[newLen]; System.arraycopy(readBuf, sz, newBuf, 0, newLen); readBuf = newBuf; }' change 'System.arraycopy(readBuf, sz, newBuf, 0, newLen);' to 'System.arraycopy(readBuf, 0, newBuf, 0, newLen);'. Trigger added to TarTestCase: public void testChunkedRead() throws Exception { byte[] expected = new byte[1000]; for (int i = 0; i < 1000; i++) expected[i] = (byte) i; ByteArrayOutputStream bytes = new ByteArrayOutputStream(); TarArchiveOutputStream tos = new TarArchiveOutputStream(bytes); TarArchiveEntry e = new TarArchiveEntry("data.bin"); e.setSize(1000); tos.putArchiveEntry(e); tos.write(expected); tos.closeArchiveEntry(); tos.close(); TarArchiveInputStream tis = new TarArchiveInputStream(new ByteArrayInputStream(bytes.toByteArray())); tis.getNextTarEntry(); ByteArrayOutputStream actual = new ByteArrayOutputStream(); byte[] chunk = new byte[100]; int n; while ((n = tis.read(chunk, 0, chunk.length)) != -1) actual.write(chunk, 0, n); assertTrue(Arrays.equals(expected, actual.toByteArray())); }  Trace: read #1 takes 100 of record 1 and keeps 412 bytes; read #2 consumes 100 of them correctly and then keeps readBuf[0..312) instead of [100..412), so read #3 returns bytes 100-199 again; deterministic. Failure text: 'junit.framework.AssertionFailedError' (no message) at TarTestCase.testChunkedRead. Collateral: existing tests read via IOUtils.copy with 8 KB buffers on small entries (single read per entry) - the remainder path is not exercised; confirm with the full suite.
ideas.gold: org.apache.commons.compress.archivers.tar.TarArchiveInputStream#read - the remainder of a partially consumed record must be copied from offset sz; the only changed line.
ideas.wrong_answer_expected: TarArchiveOutputStream#write at rank 1 (the symmetric writer-side suspect), or TarBuffer#readRecord / #readBlock; TarArchiveInputStream#skip and #getNextTarEntry as further off-path picks.
ideas.model_specificity: Claude Opus cannot see what the bytes look like (never runs the test) and reads write() and read() once each; whether it catches '0 vs sz' depends on attentive simulation - roughly even odds. GPT-5.6 may run the test and, if it prints diagnostics via a scratch class, sees the repeated 100-byte block, which points squarely at the reader remainder logic - expect GPT above Claude here.

ideas.title: JacksonCore: JsonWriteContext.reset keeps a stale index; the PARSER throws 'was expecting double-quote to start field name' on the second sibling object
ideas.mechanism: Generator-side state bug reported by the parser in a generate-then-parse round trip: the exception stack is entirely inside ReaderBasedJsonParser/ParserMinimalBase, the message is a parser complaint with a column number, and the malformed document is never shown (Source: java.io.StringReader@hash). The bug is a missing '_index = -1' in reset(int type), which only bites when a child context object is REUSED - i.e. for the second sibling container written at the same depth, several write calls after the first sibling succeeded (delayed failure). The comma decision that goes wrong is DEFINED in JsonWriteContext.writeFieldName / writeValue ('_index < 0 ? AS_IS : AFTER_COMMA') and emitted by WriterBasedJsonGenerator._writeFieldName/_verifyValueWrite, and the reuse decision lives in createChildObjectContext/createChildArrayContext - each a plausible alternative fix site ('allocate a fresh child', 'reset the index when reusing'). reset() itself reads complete: it resets _type and _currentName.
ideas.construction: Project JacksonCore-1f (/Users/shawnli/Desktop/Honours/defects4j/supervisor_pipeline_runs/core-benchmark-scaleup-v2/screening/JacksonCore, JUnit 4.8.2, JUnit3-style tests). Edit src/main/java/com/fasterxml/jackson/core/json/JsonWriteContext.java, protected final JsonWriteContext reset(int type): delete the line '_index = -1;' (keep '_type = type; _currentName = null; return this;'). Trigger added to src/test/java/com/fasterxml/jackson/core/main/TestGeneratorObject.java (neutral name): public void testNestedObjects() throws Exception { StringWriter sw = new StringWriter(); JsonGenerator gen = new JsonFactory().createGenerator(sw); gen.writeStartObject(); gen.writeFieldName("a"); gen.writeStartObject(); gen.writeFieldName("x"); gen.writeNumber(1); gen.writeEndObject(); gen.writeFieldName("b"); gen.writeStartObject(); gen.writeFieldName("y"); gen.writeNumber(2); gen.writeEndObject(); gen.writeEndObject(); gen.close(); JsonParser jp = createParserUsingReader(sw.toString()); JsonToken t; while ((t = jp.nextToken()) != null) { } jp.close(); }  (the loop is the whole assertion: the document must parse). Generated text is {"a":{"x":1},"b":{,"y":2}} because the reused child context starts at _index 0. Failure text: 'com.fasterxml.jackson.core.JsonParseException: Unexpected character (',' (code 44)): was expecting double-quote to start field name at [Source: java.io.StringReader@...; line: 1, column: 20]' at ParserMinimalBase._reportError / _reportUnexpectedChar / ReaderBasedJsonParser field-name parsing / nextToken / TestGeneratorObject.testNestedObjects. Deterministic. Collateral: any existing generator test that writes two sibling containers under one parent (arrays of arrays/objects in TestGeneratorArray, TestJsonGenerator, pretty-printer tests) will also fail - expect several; acceptable but record them.
ideas.gold: com.fasterxml.jackson.core.json.JsonWriteContext#reset - a reused child context must restart its entry index at -1; the removed line and the only behavioural change.
ideas.wrong_answer_expected: JsonWriteContext#writeFieldName or #createChildObjectContext at rank 1; WriterBasedJsonGenerator#_writeFieldName / #writeStartObject, or a parser method (ReaderBasedJsonParser#nextToken / #_handleUnusualFieldName) when the model trusts the stack.
ideas.model_specificity: Claude Opus knows the generator produced the text and follows writeStartObject -> createChildObjectContext -> reset in 3 greps; whether it notices the missing reset depends on having read writeFieldName's '_index < 0' first (order-dependent). GPT-5.6 often runs the test and can print the generated string via a scratch program, revealing '{,' at the second object, which strongly implicates the reuse path; its residual error is ownership (createChildObjectContext vs reset).

ideas.title: Chart: DefaultStatisticalCategoryDataset.remove() skips the bounds refresh for one cached extreme; the stale Range surfaces later as a single aggregate (or boolean) mismatch
ideas.mechanism: Delayed aggregate failure through a cache. remove() only recomputes the four cached extremes when the removed cell held one of them; deleting one of the four clauses (the max-including-stddev pair) leaves the remaining three-way condition looking complete. The stale value is then read back by getRangeBounds(true) as the upper bound of a Range - the failure is one Range (or a bare AssertionFailedError if asserted as a boolean), with no indication of which of the four caches is stale or which of add/remove/updateBounds maintains it. The DEFINERS of the wrong-looking quantity are updateBounds() (100 lines of min/max bookkeeping) and add(Number,Number,Comparable,Comparable) (its own inline incremental cache update), and the CONSUMERS are getRangeBounds/getRangeUpperBound - all lexically matched by 'Range'/'bounds' in the failure and all more prominent than a missing clause in remove(). Models attribute to the definer of the quantity that looks wrong.
ideas.construction: Project Chart-1f (/Users/shawnli/Desktop/Honours/defects4j/supervisor_pipeline_runs/core-benchmark-scaleup-v2/screening/Chart, JUnit 3, src dir 'source', tests dir 'tests'). ideas.title: Math Precision.round(float): sign dropped from the decimal factor upstream; the real roundUnscaled sign branches downstream look inverted
ideas.mechanism: Reverses CHART-PIE-03 with a REAL terminal. The original algorithm folds the sign into the factor (factor = 10^scale * sign) so that x*factor is a non-negative magnitude, and roundUnscaled's CEILING/FLOOR cases use `sign` to pick floor/ceil on that magnitude. If H2 defines factor WITHOUT `* sign` (a definition that reads as complete and natural), unscaled becomes negative and the CEILING case does floor(nextAfter(-123.45,-inf)) = -124 -> -1.24 instead of -1.23. The model sees 'CEILING of a negative rounded toward -inf' and the first sign-sensitive code it meets is `if (sign == -1) floor(...) else ceil(...)` in roundUnscaled, which reads exactly like an inverted sign test. The magnitude invariant is stated only in roundUnscaled's javadoc ABOVE the declaration, which Claude's `grep -n 'roundUnscaled' -A30` never shows (it prints lines after the match). Flipping the branch is a compensating edit that satisfies the one visible failing assertion, and Claude never runs tests, so nothing refutes it; GPT-5.6 runs at most the unmodified test, which still reports the same first assertion. The definer heuristic points at roundUnscaled (it defines the rounded value); H2 merely 'computes 10^scale'.

The only visible shift is in H5 `(word << shift)`, next to a `field` parameter that is applied to the holder mask but not to the word, so H5 looks like it forgot `(word & field)`. That edit passes both assertions, so arithmetic cannot refute it. Nothing in H4 'defines' a sign-extended value; the widening happens inside the call expression. In the original treatment both models found H5's shift formula and stopped; here they will find the same formula, judge it deficient, and stop.

The bug (header padding computed without the name's NUL byte) misaligns the old-binary data by one byte: the first entry's content compares unequal (bare assertTrue) or, if only counts are checked, the second getNextCPIOEntry throws IOException("Unknown magic [..]") from the READER. ideas.title: Zip extra-field registry: header-id dispatch to an inherited parser, with a real normalising override in the concrete subclass shadowing the gold
ideas.mechanism: Registry dispatch + generic same-signature names + declaring-class attribution + a visible consumer that mutates the quantity. ExtraFieldUtils keeps a real static Map<ZipShort, Class> registry; the model must decode a little-endian header id (bytes 0x75 0x70 -> 0x7075 = UnicodePathExtraField.UPATH_ID) to find the class, then discover that parseFromLocalFileData is implemented six times (AsiExtraField, AbstractUnicodeExtraField, UnrecognizedExtraField, JarMarker, the interface, and a new real override in UnicodePathExtraField). Allowed collateral: ResizableDoubleArrayTest::testAddElementRolling ADDITIVE section (the pre-existing layout comments '0,0,x,x,x,0 -- time to contract' assume the old copy-from-0 expand); validate testDiscard/testSubstitute. Gold: ResizableDoubleArray.java (1,207 lines), method expand.
ideas.gold: org.apache.commons.math3.util.ResizableDoubleArray#expand — MathArrays.compact's contract (window placed at the beginning) is fixed by its javadoc and by contract(), which uses it identically and resets startIndex; expand is the only caller that consumes the relocated window without updating the origin; repairing compact to copy from 0 instead would overflow contract()'s numElements+1 allocation.
ideas.wrong_answer_expected: org.apache.commons.math3.util.MathArrays#compact (definer of the moved layout) or ResizableDoubleArray#addElementRolling (the method that advanced startIndex) at rank 1; gold expand rank 2-3.
ideas.model_specificity: Weakest against Opus: a `grep -n startIndex ResizableDoubleArray.java` shows contract's reset and expand's omission side by side, and Claude does exactly that kind of grep. Mid-tier Claude and GPT (which reasons from the trigger's runtime values) are more likely to blame compact or addElementRolling. Included as the shared-state member of the family; expect Acc@1 0.55 Opus, 0.45 mid-tier, ~0.5 GPT.

LEX-01.why: This is a faithful lever-L1 re-instantiation of the only structure that beat both models (CHART-PIE-03, 8/8 wrong, gold rank 6 in 9/10). In every PIE-03 run the model computed the sign flip correctly and then blamed the hop where the value first diverged from the natural convention (drift: 'point1 - point2', direction-loaded identifiers, directionless javadoc) while exonerating the leaf whose body was the textbook implementation of its name ('shift simply adds the displacement, which matches its documentation'). Here the natural convention is even stronger and universally known (zone offset = local - UTC; Java ZONE_OFFSET; RFC 822), hop 2 computes instant - wall with direction-loaded identifiers (M2: Claude derived direction from identifiers alone in 4/5 runs), and the leaf's 'offsetMinutes < 0 ? '-' : '+'' is byte-for-byte the original FastDatePrinter idiom the model recalls, so it will be judged internally consistent. Both models checked callers in PIE-03 and found every hop single-use, so there is no cross-check; M3 predicts the exonerated leaf sinks below glue to rank 5-6, so the attack's MRR estimate (0.5) is optimistic. Small discount versus PIE-03 because time-zone sign is a well-known pitfall and a minority of runs may reason 'hop 2 deliberately defines UTC - local, the leaf misreads it'. Mid-tier Claude (Haiku 4.5 / Sonnet 4.6 completed runs matched Opus on ADV-DEPTH/REGISTRY) should behave similarly; its stronger depth prior occasionally lands on the leaf by accident.
LEX-01.what_would_rescue_the_model: Treating hop 2's precise @param docs (instant = UTC ms, wall = local ms) as pinning its output convention and then asking which consumer misreads a UTC-minus-local value; knowledge of sign-inverted offset conventions (POSIX TZ) prompting a boundary check; or a depth-prior fallback that puts the deepest hop first.
LEX-01.strengthening: Rename hop 2's parameters to utc and local (offset = utc - local) so the backwards operand order is visually unmistakable through direction-loaded identifiers alone (M2) while the javadoc stays precise, and fold hop 3's millis-to-minutes scaling into hop 4 so the leaf is the single sign-reading line and reads exactly like the original appendTo test.

LEX-02.why: Both models locate the first divergent value and blame the body that computes it (HA: 7/7 ranked BitField.lane first as 'the first divergent value on the path'; CONVERSION-LONG Claude evidence: 'overlay computes shift=(index+at)*width even though at is a bit position'). Here the first wrong value, shift=256, is computed inside overlay, overlay's javadoc contradicts its code (L1 says blame the doc/code contradiction), combine's call is name-aligned and reads as correct, and the depth prior also points at overlay, so the default verdict is overlay at rank 1. The rescue path is real but not default: Claude grepped all chain call sites in 1/3 CONVERSION-LONG runs and 1/3 PIE-03 runs and read shortArrayToLong as a reference in run-003; GPT always greps 'overlay(' repo-wide and infers contracts from consumer usage (L4: 7/7). A run that sees shortArrayToLong's overlay(out, word, i, dstPos, ...) beside combine's overlay(total, words[at], index, at, ...) and tracks that combine's 'index' is the bit position will flip to combine. Claude also tracks 'at = dstPos' across hops, so combine's inverted local naming may itself draw suspicion. Note EDIT 3 removes the inline 'i * 16 + dstPos' sibling oracle that both models cite in nearly every correct Conversion top-1 (L6), which slightly helps the attack.
LEX-02.what_would_rescue_the_model: A repo-wide grep for 'overlay(' revealing the two Conversion callers with (i, dstPos) order and a comparison of argument roles with combine's (index, at); or noticing that the value tracked as 'at = dstPos' through gather/compose/widen is rebound to 'index' at the widen->combine boundary and that combine's loop counter reuses the name 'at'.
LEX-02.strengthening: Name-align the two pinning callers as well (final int index = i; final int at = dstPos; NumberUtils.overlay(out, word, index, at, 16, 0xffffL)) so every call site shows an identical-looking argument list and the swap is detectable only by tracking what each local means, not by reading names.

LEX-03.why: Second L1 instance: the model recalls the canonical normalizeAngle formula 'a - TWO_PI * floor((a + PI - center)/TWO_PI)', so the leaf's 'a - correction' pattern-matches the textbook shape (exonerated, as shift was in PIE-03) while the definer's ceil-from-the-upper-edge-minus-one is the only non-canonical line on the path (HA: models rank 'the only non-canonical line' first, 7/7). A model that evaluates hop 2 finds it equals -k and phrases this as 'turnsToUpper has the sign of the standard k reversed', exactly the PIE-03 verdict. The assertTrue failure without expected/actual pushes both models to hand-simulate one pair rather than run a probe, which favours template matching. Weaker than LEX-01 because the definer is self-consistent as 'turns to add' (positive when a lies below the window) and a careful evaluator can notice removeTurns subtracts what it was told to add; also the leaf's name 'removeTurns' matches 'a - correction', which cuts both ways. Mid-tier: same template pull, similar rate.
LEX-03.what_would_rescue_the_model: Evaluating the definer on a concrete pair and recognising it consistently returns the number of turns to ADD (positive for a below the window), then checking that removeTurns subtracts; or a jshell probe of unwind/removeTurns showing the leaf inverts a correctly-signed input.
LEX-03.strengthening: Fold hop 3's scaling into the leaf so it reads 'return a - MathUtils.TWO_PI * turns;', byte-for-byte the shape of the original 'a - TWO_PI * floor(...)', making the definer the only line that does not match the remembered formula; keep the definer's javadoc directionless.

LEX-04.why: The trace frame, the exception message, the comparison and the @throws all sit in gather, and GPT greps failure vocabulary, so gather is read first and is a strong attractor. But neither hop has a non-canonical line and neither contradicts its own doc (span's doc matches count*width+at; gather's '>=' matches its message), so the models fall back to the stated contract: the message literally spells out '(nInts-1)*32+dstPos', and the sibling guards in Conversion ('(nShorts-1)*16+dstPos >= 64' in shortArrayToLong/byteArrayToLong) are the sibling oracle both models cite in almost every correct Conversion top-1 (L6: 29/29 GPT, 18/24 Claude). A model comparing span's 64 against the stated inclusive formula sees the missing '-1' and blames span, the first divergent value (HA/ADV-DEPTH pattern). Claude reads span in the same grep as the guard and may settle on 'span returns the exclusive end but the guard needs the last lsb'. Off-by-one-in-the-guard is also a common archetype, so a substantial minority will rank gather first; roughly a coin flip tilted toward the gold, slightly worse for a more trace-anchored mid-tier model.
LEX-04.what_would_rescue_the_model: Comparing span's value against the inclusive formula stated in the exception message, the facade @throws and the unchanged sibling guards ((nShorts-1)*16+dstPos), which shows span omits the '-1'; GPT's sed range over Conversion exposes all of these at once.
LEX-04.strengthening: Remove the formula from the exception message and gather's @throws (generic 'run does not fit in 64 bits') so no inclusive formula is visible near the guard, leaving only span's exclusive-end doc versus gather's '>=' and making the guard read as the off-by-one.

LEX-05.why: The wrong-looking quantity 'shift' is defined in the gold, so the definer-attribution heuristic that beat the models in PIE-03 here points AT the gold. Claude's CONVERSION-LONG evidence chains explicitly track 'at is a bit position (dstPos)' across hops and every upstream hop, the facade javadoc and the sibling oracle 'i * 16 + dstPos' say bits, so a five-against-one unit vote makes overlay's 'at * Byte.SIZE' the obvious odd one out; the self-consistent byte doc reads as a doc bug, not a caller bug. Same-depth decoys and doc tricks around a computable arithmetic error have not moved rank 1 in any prior run (HA 7/7, ADV-DEPTH 3/3 completed incl. Haiku/Sonnet). Some chance a model argues the caller should convert because the test's dstPos values (8, 16) are byte-aligned, more so for a mid-tier model leaning on the local doc.
LEX-05.what_would_rescue_the_model: Default behaviour already rescues: tracking the unit of 'at' from the facade contract and every upstream hop, and the sibling formula oracle in Conversion showing bit arithmetic; the gold is the first and only divergent line.
LEX-05.strengthening: Rename the gold's parameter to byteOffset and make the byte contract look deliberate (neighbouring NumberUtils helpers using Byte.SIZE), while renaming combine's parameter to a unit-free 'offset' so the unit is stated only at the two ends and the mismatch appears at the call boundary rather than inside the gold's body.

LEX-06.why: Verified with javac that the two single-static-imports compile and the unqualified call binds to the long-word overload, producing exactly the observed 0x0F123456 at bit 0. Both models verify arithmetic against the observed value (Claude: 'shift is 256, which Java masks to 0, giving 0x0F123456' in 3/3 runs; GPT ran jshell), and only the NumberUtils formula reproduces 252851286 (the Msb0 decoy gives shift 24 and a different value), so the decoy is refuted by computation even if the import block is never read. Type-based resolution (words is long[]) is also within reach. Risk is confined to a run that binds the call by eye, reads the strange Msb0 expression and submits without computing, plausible mainly for a mid-tier model. GPT's sed ranges usually include the import block, and Claude's grep for 'static long overlay' shows both declarations, prompting a comparison.
LEX-06.what_would_rescue_the_model: Evaluating both overloads on the trigger arguments (only (index+at)*width reproduces the failing value), noting the word type is long, or reading ObjectUtils' import block.
LEX-06.strengthening: Place the decoy overload in BitField directly below widen (the hop read immediately before combine) and give it a shift expression that also evaluates to 0 for (index 0, at 8, width 32), so arithmetic no longer discriminates and only import/type resolution does.

LEX-07.why: The attribution component is LEX-01 (same definer computing instant - wall, same textbook sign test) and inherits its PIE-03 evidence, but the gold now sits in the facade class that Claude bulk-reads first and harvests for filler ranks (77/80 Claude filler slots are facade-class siblings), so the helper is always seen and always in the top 10. Proximity slightly helps the model: a model recalling the original appendTo sees that the sign test is unchanged and the chain now hands it a negated quantity, which still blames hop 2, but with the abs/digit logic back in appendTo some runs will rank the facade or the helper first as 'the place the sign is decided'. The scorer artifact is negligible: the submit tool validates each Class::method against a catalog spelled Outer$Inner and rejects nonexistent keys, so a dotted spelling is bounced back for correction, and GPT spelled HarmonicFitter$ParameterGuesser with '$' in every observed submission. Net: a bit below LEX-01.
LEX-07.what_would_rescue_the_model: Same as LEX-01 (reading hop 2's @param docs as pinning UTC - local and checking the consumer), plus proximity: with the helper in the same class as the facade, a model that decides 'the fix belongs where the sign is chosen' lands on the gold; the catalog-validated submit tool prevents the '$' misspelling from costing anything.
LEX-07.strengthening: Place the helper at the bottom of the nested class, outside any 'appendTo -A30' window, and call it inline as designatorSign(DateFormatUtils.wallClockOffsetMinutes(calendar)) so it reads as trivial glue while the chain's definer is the only visible subtraction.

LEX-08.why: Pure lexical stripping has never moved rank 1: the 21.6x host-file experiment and the same-depth decoys changed nothing, and both models compute the gold's arithmetic regardless of naming (Claude's 'shift is 256, masked to 0' evidence appears whether or not javadoc was displayed). Here the gold's s=(i+k)*w reproduces the observed 252851286 while the decoy widen displays the correct closed-form 'i * 32 + at' one hop earlier and computes verifiably correct masks, so the two formulas sit side by side and the wrong one is the deepest, first-divergent, and only wrong-valued line. The unchanged sibling oracle in Conversion ('i * 16 + dstPos') reinforces it. Expected result: gold rank 1, widen or combine rank 2, matching the attack's own prediction.
LEX-08.what_would_rescue_the_model: Default behaviour: computing the gold's shift against the failing value and comparing with the correct shift formula visible in the decoy and in the Conversion siblings.
LEX-08.strengthening: Compute the decoy's masks with a running mask (mask = field << at; mask <<= width per iteration) so no closed-form shift expression appears anywhere but the gold, and route shortArrayToLong/byteArrayToLong through the same helper family to remove the 'i * W + dstPos' sibling oracle.

SSN-01.why: The whole attack is a class choice, and the test text leaks it: the literal "UTF-16BE", a test named testEscapesInUtf16Stream, and a class literally named UTF8StreamJsonParser all say the byte parser is not on the path. Opus knows Jackson autodetects encoding and wraps non-UTF-8 bytes in a Reader, and its observed hop-following (BaseTest.createParserUsingStream -> JsonFactory.createJsonParser -> ByteSourceJsonBootstrapper.constructParser, 2-3 greps) lands on lines 229-239 where only UTF-8 gets UTF8StreamJsonParser. The observed 'submit 0-1 calls after gold' pattern requires having SEEN a plausible fault; a model that opens the UTF-8 twin sees a correct method, has no fault to submit, and the only other parser class is the obvious next lead; `grep -rn _decodeEscaped` then shows both twins and the missing `++` at ReaderBasedJsonParser:1769 matches the failure (escape selector re-emitted as 'a\ttb'). Weak Claude is likelier to submit the UTF-8 twin as 'the escape decoder' without that second check.
SSN-01.what_would_rescue_the_model: Reading ByteSourceJsonBootstrapper.constructParser (two hops from the test helper), a repository-wide grep for _decodeEscaped that shows both twins side by side, or simply trusting the 'UTF-16BE' cue in the test.
SSN-01.strengthening: Verified in this checkout: JsonFactory._createJsonParser passes isEnabled(CANONICALIZE_FIELD_NAMES) as `canonicalize`, and constructParser line 233 only builds UTF8StreamJsonParser `if (canonicalize)`; otherwise UTF-8 bytes ALSO go to ReaderBasedJsonParser. Use `f.disable(JsonFactory.Feature.CANONICALIZE_FIELD_NAMES)` with createParserUsingStream(f, JSON, "UTF-8") and a test name without 'Utf16' so every surface cue says UTF-8 stream while the Reader twin runs; expect Opus p_wrong to rise to ~0.5.

SSN-02.why: The dispatch is not hidden from a hop-follower: the test's very first call is MatrixUtils.createRealMatrix(data), whose body (lines 127-135) is three lines with `data.length * data[0].length <= 4096` in plain view, and n=70 is a conspicuous literal (4900 > 4096 is trivial). Once in BlockRealMatrix.getRow the transposed index is refutable by arithmetic exactly as in the hypothesis-ambiguity experiment: the failure value 852 = data[8][52] is block (0,1) at iRow 8, and getColumn/getEntry in the same grep window use iBlock*blockColumns+jBlock. Only two concrete getRow definitions exist in linear/ (AbstractRealMatrix, BlockRealMatrix), so even a repository grep hits the gold. The wrong branch requires skipping the 3-line factory, assuming Array2DRowRealMatrix, and then submitting AbstractRealMatrix.getRow despite finding nothing wrong in it, which is plausible for a weak model but rare for Opus.
SSN-02.what_would_rescue_the_model: Reading createRealMatrix (3 lines, first call in the test), or `grep -rn 'getRow('` which returns only the two implementations.
SSN-02.strengthening: Remove the dimension from the test source: load the 70x70 data from a test resource file (Math tests already use resources) or an existing helper, so `n*n > 4096` cannot be evaluated by reading the test. Claude never runs code, so the dispatch becomes invisible unless it opens BOTH MatrixUtils and the fixture.

SSN-07.why: Stack-trace anchoring is the shared bias and the entire signal is in ZipFile, but the reader (resolveLocalFileHeaderData lines 499-537, populateFromCentralDirectory) contains no implausible line, and the test itself names the writer, so a hop-follower with nothing to blame goes to ZipArchiveOutputStream. `grep -n offsets` there returns 4 lines; line 660 `offsets.put(ze, ZipLong.getBytes(written + WORD))` sits directly above `writeOut(LFH_SIG); written += WORD;` under the field comment 'offsets of the LFH starts' -- an arithmetic anomaly of exactly the kind both models refute in one look. Opus knows the CFH offset field points at the LFH signature and that 26 is the correct filename-length offset, so it will not blame LFH_OFFSET_FOR_FILENAME_LENGTH. Weak Claude, unable to verify spec constants, may stop at the reader (skipBytes loop) and rank the throwing frame first.
SSN-07.what_would_rescue_the_model: One grep for `offsets` in the writer; knowledge that ZipFile is the spec-correct side; for GPT, running the test and inspecting the produced archive (unzip -l / hexdump).
SSN-07.strengthening: Keep the put line canonical (`ZipLong.getBytes(written)`) and move it one statement down, after `writeOut(LFH_SIG); written += WORD;`, so no line reads wrong and only the ordering is; additionally pick an entry name whose first two bytes decode to a small filename length so the misread lands in ExtraFieldUtils.parse ('data starting at 0 is in unknown format'), giving the reader a plausible-looking culprit deeper in the trace.

SSN-05.why: This is the only attack built on the one mechanism with a measured double failure (definer attribution), and the field-mediated link genuinely stops a next-symbol grep at getMaximumExplodePercent. But the inserted cache has a small footprint: `grep -n maximumExplodePercent` returns the field, the getter's write, the datasetChanged reset to -1.0 and the setter's Math.max side by side; the test's narrative is 'lower a percentage, redraw' and Math.max cannot lower -- an immediate semantic refutation. The realistic wrong rank-1 is getMaximumExplodePercent because 'remove the cache' is a defensible fix and the stale value is defined there; that is a real ownership split rather than a search failure, so the attack works only through rank order, as the author says.
SSN-05.what_would_rescue_the_model: Grepping the field name (one call) and matching the setter's monotone update to the test's 'lowered' action.
SSN-05.strengthening: Make the setter's update read as an idiomatic incremental max (`if (percent > this.maximumExplodePercent) this.maximumExplodePercent = percent;`, no Math.max), route the correct invalidation through Plot's existing datasetChanged path rather than a visible -1.0 reset adjacent to the setter, and have the test lower a non-max key first, then the max holder, so the 'lowering' cue is diluted. Remember transient doubles deserialize to 0.0, so readObject must reset to -1.0 or testSerialization breaks.

SSN-06.why: The lexical cue is decisive: '&#x' names the only translator whose source mentions hex, and every plausible blame line (the missing isHex term in the return at line 136, or the semiNext logic) lives inside the gold method, so within-class attribution cannot miss. The lightning rod `pos += Character.charCount(Character.codePointAt(input, pt))` is real in this checkout, but for the ASCII trigger it is harmless, and Opus's arithmetic (six chars in 'A', return of 5) resolves the leftover ';' directly; the second assertion ('A b') confirms one-char under-consumption, the same refutation pattern seen in the hypothesis-ambiguity experiment. Weak Claude, which reads less of the 60-line method, is more likely to grab the visible loop bug.
SSN-06.what_would_rescue_the_model: Counting consumed characters against the return value; the CharSequenceTranslator contract comment that translate returns codepoints consumed.
SSN-06.strengthening: Keep causality intact but make the base loop look responsible: append a supplementary character after the entity ('A😀') so the failure shows a surrogate pair beside the leftover ';' and the `codePointAt(input, pt)` indexing looks implicated. Verified: with the bug the output is 'A;<pair>', and fixing the gold alone (return 6) yields 'A<pair>', so the gold stays the sole fix.

SSN-08.why: As specified the attack does not fire: PaddedNumberField's constructor throws IllegalArgumentException for size < 3, so 'SSS' -> padding 3 -> `padding - 1` = 2 throws inside FastDateFormat.getInstance, and the trace names selectNumberRule one frame above the throw -- a giveaway. With a 4-letter token (SSSS: '005' vs '0005', or yyyy with a 3-digit year) it fires as intended. Then the dispatcher is a 9-line switch two greps from the test (`case 'S'` at line 231 -> selectNumberRule at 356) and `padding - 1` is unmistakable once seen. PaddedNumberField.appendTo is the definer-bias decoy, but its loop pads exactly to mSize and Opus computes it; Claude's habit of grepping the named symbol with -A30 shows the whole switch.
SSN-08.what_would_rescue_the_model: Grepping selectNumberRule or MILLISECOND in FastDatePrinter (one call after locating parsePattern).
SSN-08.strengthening: After fixing the trigger, choose a value that exercises appendTo's cryptic else branch (millis >= 100 with SSSS: '123' vs '0123', `digits = 3; for (i = mSize; --i >= digits;)`) so the definer PaddedNumberField.appendTo looks like the culprit, and name the test after padding rather than rule selection.

SSN-04.why: The registry hop costs one grep ('756' or '0x75' hits AsiExtraField.HEADER_ID), and the decoder body then shows `uid = ZipShort.getValue(tmp, 8); gid = ZipShort.getValue(tmp, 8);` on consecutive lines -- a duplicated offset any model flags immediately, corroborated by the class javadoc table (UID then GID) and the encoder 150 lines above writing offsets 6 and 8. The definer bias toward getLocalFileDataData needs the encoder to look inconsistent; it matches the documented layout, so the same-file comparison both models perform resolves to the decoder.
SSN-04.what_would_rescue_the_model: Reading parseFromLocalFileData (the duplicate offset 8), or the javadoc layout table at the top of the file.
SSN-04.strengthening: Swap the reads (uid from 8, gid from 6) instead of duplicating an offset, so each line is individually plausible and the round-trip diff reads as a uid/gid swap either side could own; the encoder then defines the mismatched bytes and CRC with no local tell in the decoder.

SSN-03.why: Two construction defects as written: (1) a 1204-char document fits the 2000-char Reader token buffer with no escape, so _finishString takes the resetWithShared fast path and size() returns _inputLen = 1200 -- the bug never executes; the string needs an escape sequence (or >2000 chars) to reach _finishString2; (2) getText() before getTextLength() caches _resultString and size() then returns its length, so the length assertion must come first. Once fixed, the model greps `_segmentSize` (9 hits) and sees `finishCurrentSegment: _segmentSize += _currentSize` beside `expand: _segmentSize += curr.length`, with `_currentSize = 0` two lines later -- the deepest-visible-arithmetic pattern the chain experiments show both models resolve in the gold's favour. The competing owner (_finishString2 should call setCurrentLength) is weaker than in-class sibling evidence.
SSN-03.what_would_rescue_the_model: One grep for _segmentSize, or reading expand() directly below finishCurrentSegment.
SSN-03.strengthening: Assert via getTextCharacters()/getTextOffset() instead of getTextLength() so the failure is an ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException thrown inside TextBuffer.buildResultArray/contentsAsArray (which sizes the array from size() then copies full segments) -- a throwing frame that DEFINES the array, pulling stack-trace and definer bias onto a different TextBuffer method while the gold stays finishCurrentSegment.

OWN-01.why: This is a re-hosting of the only construction both models failed, with the mechanism intact: the definer's body (inner - outer) contradicts the natural reading of 'displacement between the unexploded and exploded points' (outer - inner), while the consumer's '+' matches 'translate by'. Claude's actual PIE-03 greps (`grep -n "drift(" -A25`, `-B2/-B3` at most) showed bodies with little or no javadoc and it still ranked drift first 3/3; the evidence chains say explicitly 'drift most likely has the reversed subtraction, shift simply adds the displacement'. With p1.x=100, p2.x=50 both fixes are trigger-equivalent (87.5 either way), so simulation cannot break the tie and the coherence heuristic decides. The pin is invisible to Claude in the common path (0/56 test greps). The only new rescue is that Claude in run-001 did a repo-wide caller grep within source (`grep -rn "\.shift(\|nudge(\|drift(..." source`), which in this design would surface PiePlot.drawLeftLabel/drawRightLabel's second use of displacement(); about a third of runs might see it, and only some of those would infer that the second caller pins the convention. Hence slightly below the designer's 0.88-0.9.
OWN-01.what_would_rescue_the_model: Seeing the second production caller (drawLeftLabel's `elbow + displacement(link, elbow)`) or RectangleAnchorTests#testDisplacement and inferring that the definer's inner-minus-outer convention is fixed; or recalling JFreeChart's real getArcBounds (deltaX = (p1 - p2) * pct; `unexploded.getX() - deltaX`) and recognising that the chain preserved the definer's convention and flipped the consumer's operator.
OWN-01.strengthening: Make the definer read reversed and the gold read canonical from the bodies alone, since Claude rarely sees javadoc: name the two-point core's parameters after the test's vocabulary (`displacement(Point2D unexplodedPoint, Point2D explodedPoint)` returning unexploded - exploded) and give the gold `translate(Rectangle2D area, double dx, double dy)` with '@return the area translated by (dx, dy)'; and keep the production pin out of Claude's caller-grep path by routing drawLeftLabel/drawRightLabel through the 4-arg overload's package-private sibling rather than a bare `displacement(` call, leaving the unit test as the primary pin.

OWN-02.why: The structure matches PIE-03 (sign defined in one hop, applied in another, both one-line fixes trigger-equivalent on every assertion: 0+(-1)*1 = -1 and -10+6 = -4 either way) and Claude's -A greps will show `return whole < 0 ? 1 : -1;` next to `return scaled + borrow * (long) numerator;`, which reads as 'inverted sign, canonical combine' and fires the definer heuristic. Three things weaken it relative to PIE-03: the definer's javadoc states its values explicitly, so there is no doc/body contradiction to latch onto; the name `borrow` itself licenses subtraction in the consumer (borrow = 1 means 'we borrow', so `+ borrow * numerator` is the odd operator), which a contract reader turns against the gold; and the memorised real code (`whole * den - numerator` when whole < 0) is consistent with blaming the consumer. Because the chain is two hops plus a sibling, both models read everything in 3-4 calls and have the budget to reason contractually. Expect a split tilted toward the definer, more so for the weaker model.
OWN-02.what_would_rescue_the_model: Reading `borrow` semantically (a borrow sense of 1 for a negative whole means the numerator is subtracted, so `combine` should subtract), recalling that Fraction subtracts the numerator for negative wholes, or a repo grep for `borrow(` that hits ObjectUtilsTest#testBorrow.
OWN-02.strengthening: Replace the subtraction-connoting name and javadoc with a sign-neutral one (`sense(int whole)`: 'Returns the orientation of a proper numerator relative to its whole: 1 when the whole is negative, -1 otherwise') so nothing in the definer licenses subtraction in the consumer, and write the gold as `scaled + sense * (long) numerator` so it reads as the canonical combine; let the pin test alone fix the convention.

OWN-03.why: The memory pull is real: `p * (n + 1) / 100 - 1` looks like a spurious `- 1` to any model with Percentile.evaluate memorised, and `intPos - 1` looks like the remembered line; on the trigger inputs both fixes are trigger-equivalent (p=50: pos 1.5 vs 2.5 both give 2.5), so simulation cannot separate them. But the gold as specified is internally inconsistent in a way the observed coherence heuristic catches: its own guards `pos < 0 -> sorted[0]` and `pos >= n - 1 -> sorted[n - 1]` are zero-based while its indexing is one-based, and the definer's javadoc says 'zero-based' outright. In PIE-03 the models blamed the hop whose body contradicted its (ambiguous) doc; here the definer's body matches an explicit doc and the gold contradicts its own guards. Opus, which reads the whole method body in one -A grep, will see the guards; the weaker model is more likely to stop at 'the -1 deviates from Commons Math'. The related testPercentile AIOOBE (index -1) is also a consumer-side symptom if noticed.
OWN-03.what_would_rescue_the_model: Noticing the zero-based guards inside interpolate, reading the definer's 'zero-based' javadoc, or reasoning from the p=30 ArrayIndexOutOfBounds: -1 that the consumer subtracts one from a zero-based position.
OWN-03.strengthening: Move the two edge guards out of the gold into the facade (Percentile#evaluate, expressed in its own terms) so the gold's body is exactly the memorised two-line interpolation with no zero-based tell, and soften the definer's javadoc from 'zero-based fractional position' to 'fractional position counted from the first element of the sorted sample', keeping StatUtilsTest#testPercentilePosition as the pin.

OWN-04.why: Memory does make the definer's `/ dev.length` look deviant and the gold's `n / ((n - 1) * (n - 2))` look familiar, but unlike PIE-03 the two fixes are not trigger-equivalent and the failure carries a loud magnitude cue that needs no test run: 0.0700 / 1.4374 = 0.0487 is essentially the gold's factor 22/(21*20) = 0.052 applied to an O(1) g1, whereas n -> n-1 in the definer changes g1 by sqrt(n/(n-1)) ~ 1.02 and cannot produce a 20x shortfall. Opus does in-head arithmetic (it computed 112.5 in PIE-03) and both Claude tiers know the textbook G1 = sqrt(n(n-1))/(n-2) * g1, which the gold's javadoc practically invites by naming g1 and G1. The definer's explicit 'biased (population)' javadoc makes it doc-consistent, so the coherence heuristic points at the gold, not the definer. The weaker model may still stop at 'should be n-1' or blame the standardisation hop, hence the higher figure for it.
OWN-04.what_would_rescue_the_model: Any magnitude check (a 20x error cannot come from n versus n-1 in the moments), or recall of the population-to-sample conversion sqrt(n(n-1))/(n-2), which the gold's javadoc names.
OWN-04.strengthening: Remove formula vocabulary from both javadocs (gold: 'Applies the finite-sample correction for a sample of size n'; definer: 'Returns the central moment of the given order of an array of deviations', without 'biased/population') so only memory guides the reader, and trigger with a small-n test (n=5: buggy factor 0.417 vs correct 1.49, ratio 0.28) so the magnitude cue is far less diagnostic than the 0.049 ratio on the 22-value array.

OWN-05.why: The observed heuristic, blame the method that DEFINES the wrong-looking quantity, points at the gold here rather than away from it: the 0-based month is defined in dosFields by `c.get(Calendar.MONTH)`, the single most recognised off-by-one gotcha in Java, and `cal.get(Calendar.MONTH) + 1` is an idiom every model reaches for at the extraction site. Memory of the real toDosTime (`int month = time.getMonth() + 1;` beside the packing) reinforces attribution to extraction, and a -B grep that shows the javadoc ('month (1-12, as stored in the DOS date word)') makes the producer contradict its own contract. The only pull toward the packer is the design analogy with `year - 1980` living there, which is an argument about where a correction ought to live rather than a wrong-looking body; both tiers know the difference between a Java Calendar quirk and a DOS-format transform. The 1<<21 difference is decoded instantly by both, so discovery is not the issue.
OWN-05.what_would_rescue_the_model: Its default behaviour: recognising Calendar.MONTH as 0-based and placing the +1 where the Calendar is read, or reading the producer's 1-12 javadoc.
OWN-05.strengthening: Make every format-level correction visibly live in the packer so the missing month correction reads as one more packer omission: move `seconds >> 1`, `year - 1980`, and the field masks (`& 0x1f`, `& 0x0f`) into ZipShort#dosDate/dosTime, have the producer return raw Calendar fields with a javadoc that omits the '1-12' phrase ('@return the calendar fields of the given time: year, month, day, hours, minutes, seconds'), and keep the gold pinned only by the decoder symmetry test.

OWN-06.why: Jackson is heavily memorised: `_tokenInputCol = _inputPtr - _currInputRowStart - 1` and the `// convert from 0-based to 1-based` comment with `(col < 0) ? col : (col + 1)` are both recognisable real lines, so the model sees getTokenColumnNr as genuine and the new helper as the altered site without ever opening _skipWSOrEnd. The helper's own javadoc ('whose first character has just been consumed') hands a contract reader the -1 directly, and getCurrentLocation's `+ 1 // 1-based` on a past-the-char pointer is consistent with the field being 0-based. The coherence heuristic that hurt the gold in PIE-03 favours it here: the real comment explains its +1, the helper's body contradicts its own javadoc. The weaker model is somewhat more likely to stop at the visible +1 or to blame nextToken/row-start maintenance, hence its higher figure, but the gold sits one grep away from the failing assertion.
OWN-06.what_would_rescue_the_model: Memory of the real assignment line, the javadoc phrase about the consumed first character, or the observation that getCurrentLocation already does the same +1 conversion on the same pointer.
OWN-06.strengthening: Strip the pointer semantics from the helper's javadoc ('Returns the 0-based column of the current token given the buffer pointer and the row start') with neutral parameter names `(int ptr, int rowStart)`, and add the optional TextBuffer#columnOf hop so the arithmetic is not adjacent to the assignment line the model remembers; memory of the `- 1` will still rescue many runs.

OWN-07.why: Claude's first grep anchors on `intToHex(`, so the facade is the first thing it reads, and the swapped call `overlay(src, dstPos, dstInit, srcPos, nHexs)` sits directly under a signature naming `srcPos, dstInit, dstPos` in the other order; the mismatch is visible without javadoc, unlike PIE-03 where the defect needed a semantic reading of a subtraction. The failing case already tells the model 'positions crossed' (a digit written at index 0 instead of 3, taken from bit offset 3), and overlay's parameter names `from`/`at` confirm which side violates the contract. The depth prior pushed blame deeper in the chains only because the facade was a pure delegate; here the facade is the only non-trivial line and the hops are coherent. GPT-style javadoc reading is not even required.
OWN-07.what_would_rescue_the_model: Its default behaviour: aligning the facade's argument list with its own parameter list, or with overlay's `from`/`at` names.
OWN-07.strengthening: Reorder overlay's signature to `overlay(int value, int at, String into, int from, int count)` (at = character index in `into`, from = bit offset in `value`) so the facade call `overlay(src, srcPos, dstInit, dstPos, nHexs)` reads as a straight pass-through while still violating overlay's contract; the swap is then visible only to a reader who aligns overlay's parameter names, and the coherence heuristic tends to blame overlay's odd parameter order instead of the facade.

CTX-01.why: Every Claude run on the CONVERSION-LONG chain followed the same script: read each hop with a -B3/-A30 window, compute the actual value by hand, and put the hop whose formula is locally inconsistent at rank 1 (evidence chains literally say 'overlay computes shift=(index+at)*width even though at is a bit position'). Here the locally inconsistent formula is again in overlay (`m = mask << (index*width)` vs `shift = at + index*width`), the arithmetic confirms it (0x12345600 is exactly (word<<8) & 0xFFFFFFFF), and the second assertion (at=16, one word) is satisfied by both fixes so nothing refutes it. The gold line `(1L << width) - 1` in compose is the verbatim template line the model has already accepted as correct in 6/6 prior runs, and the only evidence of a positioned-mask contract sits in BitField.setValue, off the chain. Depth prior and the 'wrong-looking formula' heuristic point at the same wrong hop, which is the strongest configuration in the observed data (PIE-03 shows the definer heuristic beats depth when they disagree; here they agree).
CTX-01.what_would_rescue_the_model: The post-chain usage grep Claude ran in ~20-30% of runs (`grep -rn "overlay(\|combine(\|widen(\|..." src/main/java`) would show `NumberUtils.overlay(holder, value, 0, _shift_count, Integer.bitCount(_mask), _mask)` in BitField.setValue; an Opus that knows BitField's `_mask` is positioned would then infer overlay expects a positioned mask and move to compose. GPT-5.6 is more exposed to this rescue because it grepped `overlay(` repo-wide and compiled probe code in CONVERSION-LONG run-001. Reading the `@param mask the mask selecting the first value` tag as 'within the holder' is a weaker second rescue.
CTX-01.strengthening: Rename overlay's/widen's/combine's last parameter from `mask` to `field` and document it as 'the field of the first value' (the template's existing vocabulary), and make compose's javadoc say 'derives the value width and the field of the first value'; then the only positional word in the whole chain is overlay's `at`, which reinforces the 'forgot at in the mask shift' reading, and the BitField.setValue call site (`..., _shift_count, Integer.bitCount(_mask), _mask`) reads less obviously as a positioned mask being passed as a 'field'.

CTX-02.why: The model sees `at` applied twice and must pick the redundant one. Overlay's two lines are mutually consistent (`m = field << (at+index*width)` and `word << (at+index*width)`), so removing `at` from the word shift leaves an asymmetric method, whereas removing widen's shift leaves everything symmetric; models prefer the symmetric repair. The method name `widen` plus the `0xffffffffL &` zero-extension idiom makes a `<< at` in that line look out of place, and PIE-03 shows both models blame the hop that introduces the odd quantity (drift, 8/8) over the hop that consumes it. The contract that saves the gold is the summary sentence of widen's javadoc, which sits above the `@param` block and outside Claude's -B3 window in about two thirds of its hop reads. Against the attack: the gold is the deepest hop, and Claude's depth habit plus the run-in-three where it widens the window (n-15, -B12) rescue it often enough that this is not near-certain.
CTX-02.what_would_rescue_the_model: Seeing widen's javadoc summary ('to the given field at the given position'), which happens when Claude uses a wider pre-context (1 run in 3) and almost always for GPT-5.6's sed ranges; or reasoning that the mask line in overlay already positions by `at`, so words arriving pre-positioned is the design that keeps mask and word aligned.
CTX-02.strengthening: Move the positioning contract one hop up into ArrayUtils.gather's javadoc ('widens each value to its field at the destination position, then composes the run') and leave widen's own javadoc neutral ('Widens the values of a run.'); the contract is then read first and forgotten, widen's `<< at` is seen with no local justification, and ownership still rests on documented text.

CTX-03.why: Two y-flips (H1 `screenAngle = -angle`, H5 `centre.getY() - oy`) and the x and angle-0 assertions pass, so the model knows exactly one flip is redundant and must choose. Without H1's javadoc a bare negation in a method called `webPoint` in class `Rotation` reads as the unexplained sign, while `y - oy` is the Java2D idiom every model has written; PIE-03 behaviour (blame where the sign is introduced) then points at H1. But the H1 javadoc is the explicit explanation, and whenever Claude widens its pre-context (about 1 run in 3) or GPT reads the block, the redundant flip becomes H5. Opus also plausibly remembers the real SpiderWebPlot.getWebPoint (`-Math.sin`), which makes the negation-of-angle stage look like a legitimate rewrite and pulls attention back to displace. Net effect is close to a coin flip, slightly favouring the attack for a weaker model that reads fewer javadocs.
CTX-03.what_would_rescue_the_model: Reading H1's javadoc ('Java2D's y-axis points down ... the angle is negated'), noticing that displace adds ox but subtracts oy against a doc that says 'displaced by the given offsets', or grepping displace's callers and finding the (optional) additive PolarPlot rewire.
CTX-03.strengthening: Express the flip at H1 through the real library constant instead of a bare minus, e.g. `double screenAngle = angle * Rotation.CLOCKWISE.getFactor();` with the same javadoc, and word displace's javadoc as 'Returns the screen point displaced from the centre by the given offsets' — the named constant marks H1 as 'the place the sign was chosen' (what models blame), and 'screen point' primes the y-down reading of `y - oy` while the doc still says additive displacement.

CTX-04.why: The decoy is genuinely strong: the facade's real javadoc ('swaped with setting swapHalfWord=true') contradicts `if (!swapHalfWord)`, Claude fixated on exactly such a doc/code disagreement in PIE-03 run-001, in Compress it cats whole facade files so the javadoc is always in view, and flipping the facade's condition passes all three assertions under the buggy reader (I verified: {1,2,3,4} unswapped -> LE halfwords 0x0201,0x0403 -> 0x02010403; true -> swapped -> 0x01020304; {1,2} -> 0x0201), while halfwordAt sits beside ZipShort.getValue, which is identically little-endian house style. Against it: Claude traced exact values in every run, and the expected 0x02010403 is literally the swapped array {2,1,4,3} read big-endian, a very natural 'the facade did its job, the reader undid it' inference; facade-first attribution has happened 1/61 times; and the model may spread its doubt onto wordValue/fromHalfwords ('caller of an LE reader') rather than the facade, which still counts as wrong. I expect the top-1 to split roughly evenly between halfwordAt and the facade/wordValue group.
CTX-04.what_would_rescue_the_model: Value tracing that notices the expected value equals the post-swap array read big-endian (facade consistent with the test, deep reader not); the depth prior; treating code+test as authoritative over a stale javadoc.
CTX-04.strengthening: Order the test so the 2-byte case fails first: `assertEquals(0x0201L, CpioUtil.byteArray2long(new byte[]{1,2}, false))` gives `expected:<513> but was:<258>`, a pure 'two bytes swapped' signature that maps directly onto the facade's swap flag and gives no hint that a halfword-composition stage exists; keep the 4-byte assertions after it.

CTX-05.why: The gold is a locally visible mistake: a variable named `digits` assigned the full `length`, with `@param length the width of the field including its two terminator bytes` sitting in the last javadoc lines that Claude's -B3 window shows (octalDigits is void, so `@param length` and `*/` are the lines immediately above the declaration). Claude cats TarUtils.java whole in Compress runs, so it has the two terminator writes in view when it reads octalDigits, and its habit of computing the exact bytes ('  100644' vs '100644 \0') leads straight to 'digits should be length - 2'. rightAligned does exactly what its `@param digits` says, and the facade is untouched original code; both alternatives contradict a visible doc. The depth prior toward rightAligned and the natural 'facade should pass length-2' fix keep this from being negligible, but the observed careful-arithmetic behaviour of both models works against it.
CTX-05.what_would_rescue_the_model: Seeing `@param length ... including its two terminator bytes` in the -B3 window (very likely), the `digits = length` alias itself, or knowing the USTAR octal field layout.
CTX-05.strengthening: Remove the alias so the gold is a pure pass-through with no 'digits' concept to catch the eye: `ArArchiveOutputStream.rightAligned(value, buf, offset, length)` (bug = forwarding length instead of length - 2), and move the 'including its two terminator bytes' sentence from the `@param length` tag into the javadoc summary line so it is outside Claude's -B3 window; ownership is unchanged (octalDigits receives a width, its callee wants a digit count).

CTX-06.why: 8/8 runs already rank drift first, and only Claude run-001 used a doc argument; runs 002/003 and all five GPT runs blamed drift purely because p1-p2 is where the sign is defined, with commands (`grep -rn "drift(" -A25`, `-B2 -A25`) that never showed drift's summary sentence. The rewrite changes only that summary, which the majority of runs do not read, so the majority outcome is unchanged. For the minority that does read it, the new docs make every hop consistent with itself (drift points inward as documented, nudge scales, shift 'translates by a displacement' and adds), so a doc-reading model must decide who owes the negation and the wording ('displaced against this vector' at drift; 'translates by' at shift) points at nudge at least as much as at shift. Either way shift at rank 1 stays rare; the residual is Opus recalling the original getArcBounds subtraction at the rectangle-construction stage.
CTX-06.what_would_rescue_the_model: Reading drift's new javadoc and then choosing shift over nudge (roughly a coin flip given shift's own doc says 'translates by a displacement'), or recalling the original PiePlot.getArcBounds where the subtraction lived at the final Rectangle2D construction.
CTX-06.strengthening: Word shift's javadoc so it, not nudge, owns the exploded-direction semantics while remaining non-pointing: 'Resolves the bounds of the exploded section from the unexploded area and its scaled drift' (drop 'translates by a displacement'), and keep nudge as 'Scales the drift by the explode percentage'; this keeps the gold contractually defensible for the doc-reading minority without adding any doc/code mismatch that the definer heuristic could latch onto.

CTX-07.why: Same commuting-sign structure as CTX-03, but the sign is introduced through a named library constant (`Rotation.CLOCKWISE.getFactor()`), which models read as a deliberate choice they can question, and the real MeterPlot.valueToAngle (which Opus plausibly remembers) subtracts, so `baseAngle - sweep` looks like the original line and the factor like the intruder; the lower-bound assertion passing (sweep 0) confirms the base-angle decoy is innocent, focusing the choice on sweep vs angleAt. The counterweight is the sweep javadoc: as written ('the meter runs clockwise, so the sweep carries the Rotation#CLOCKWISE sign') it reads like a @return tag, which is exactly the part of the block Claude's -B3 window shows; a model that sees 'the sign is intended' one line above the declaration, plus angleAt's 'reached from the base angle by the given sweep', will pick angleAt. That makes Opus roughly even and a weaker, less doc-reading model somewhat more fooled.
