CTX-07.what_would_rescue_the_model: Seeing the CLOCKWISE sentence in sweep's javadoc tail via -B3, reading angleAt's doc ('reached by the given sweep' implies addition), or opening PiePlot/SpiderWebPlot and noticing the library combines Rotation factors additively.
CTX-07.strengthening: Move the sign sentence out of the @return tag into the javadoc summary line of sweep and keep @return terse ('@return the sweep'), so the -B3 window shows nothing about the sign; additionally have dialAngle (H1) pass `Rotation.CLOCKWISE` down as a parameter and let sweep multiply by `direction.getFactor()`, so the sign appears to be chosen at hop 1 and applied at hop 3, spreading the 'definer' across two decoys above the gold.

FSIG-01.why: This is the closest replica of the only observed failure and deserves credit for it, but it is weaker than PIE-03 in one decisive way. In PIE-03 the winning decoy (drift) had a javadoc-vs-code tension ('displacement from unexploded to exploded' vs p1-p2) and the gold's doc matched its code; both models cited exactly that tension. Here the tension sits at the GOLD: overlay's doc says 'index above the lead' while lead+index*width puts index 0 AT the lead, and three hops (widen/combine/overlay) document lead consistently, so compose's at-width is doc-consistent. Both models read every hop before ranking (Claude 6 calls, all 5 bodies, in every CONVERSION-LONG run) and both simulate with concrete values; simulating at=0 gives lead=-32 and a negative shift, which is a strong smell pulling toward compose, so the outcome hinges on whether the model trusts the documented lead convention. The missing numbers matter less than claimed for Claude, which never saw failure text anyway; they matter for GPT, which runs the test and here gets only 'AssertionError'. Net: a genuine coin-flip-plus for Opus, worse for a mid-tier model that stops on the first negative intermediate.
FSIG-01.what_would_rescue_the_model: Reading the three consistent '@param lead the position of the field immediately below the run' docs plus overlay's 'above the lead', then simulating lead+(index+1)*width = 0, 32 for at=0 and concluding the convention is fine and only overlay is off by one field; also noticing longToIntArray is the untouched original and so the forward chain must be at fault.
FSIG-01.strengthening: Move the doc/code tension onto the definer the way PIE-03 had it: keep compose's javadoc as '@param at the position in the result at which the first value is placed' and '@return the composed value, beginning at {@code at}', but relocate the explanatory sentence about the run being stacked above the field ending at at OUT of compose and into BitField.widen's javadoc, so a one-grep reader of compose sees an unexplained 'at - width' passed as a position; and change overlay's doc to the neutral 'at the position derived from its index and the lead' so the gold no longer carries the only visible doc/code mismatch.

FSIG-02.why: Strongest coarse-signal/indirect-flow design in the set: 2,600 lines across two classes, every stack frame in the decoder, a zero-content 'CRC error' message, and the RLE1 '4 then count' convention visibly DEFINED in setupNoRandPartB/C (the PIE-03 lever). Two things temper it. First, Claude is shown no failure text and has never run the test, so it never sees the decoder stack unless this signal-free round trip changes its habit; it then faces a pure search over encoder vs decoder with no direction, and its natural first read is the encoder's write()/writeRun() because that is where the test's input enters. Second, writeRun is locally self-checking: four explicit block[last+1]=currentChar statements followed by (char)(runLength-3) lets a model verify 4+(runLength-3)!=runLength without knowing bzip2, and the 'CRC' grep the designer notes lands on mCrc.updateCRC inside writeRun. GPT, which ran the test 10/10 times and greps repository-wide for failure vocabulary, is more likely to open writeRun and knows the format. So the gold is discoverable and locally verifiable; the attack's yield comes from models that never reach it or that trust the decoder frames.
FSIG-02.what_would_rescue_the_model: Opening writeRun (via a 'CRC' or 'runLength' grep or by reading write(int) first) and counting the four literal copies against the count byte; or reasoning that a fixture-decoding test path is stable and a round-trip CRC mismatch most often means the encoder emitted a different byte sequence than it checksummed.
FSIG-02.strengthening: Relocate the bug from the locally checkable count byte to the second RLE stage in generateMTFValues (the RUNA/RUNB zero-run emission with zPend), where an off-by-one in the bijective base-2 emission also yields decoded-content divergence and the same 'BZip2 CRC error' in the decoder, but the arithmetic cannot be verified by counting statements and the decoder's mirror (the RUNA/RUNB expansion in getAndMoveToFrontDecode) is the only visible DEFINITION of the convention.

FSIG-03.why: The trace holds (I verified parseOctal returns 0 on the NUL fields, so the 88-'b' record parses as a size-0 header and count is 4). The attack's real strength is the three-way ownership split (closeEntry vs putNextEntry vs write) and the absent-line shape, not the reader detour: Claude sees no failure text, so it never learns count was 4 and has no reason to prefer the reader; it reads the methods the test calls (putArchiveEntry, write, closeArchiveEntry) and getNextTarEntry, roughly 8-10 calls. Its habitual 'grep -n assemLen' then lists every site and makes the missing reset in closeEntry countable, exactly as GPT's wide greps did in CONVERSION-LONG. The observed models resolve behavioural ownership ambiguity by contract, and 'flush the assembly buffer but leave its length' is a classic that points at closeEntry, though putNextEntry's visible currBytes=0 is a credible rival. GPT runs the test, sees expected:<3> but was:<4>, and can infer an extra record; it has often shown 3-6 verification calls, enough to reach the writer.
FSIG-03.what_would_rescue_the_model: A single grep for assemLen showing write() resets it in its crossing branch while closeEntry flushes assemBuf without clearing assemLen; reasoning that entry-2 content is prefixed by entry-1's tail, which is a writer-side symptom regardless of what the reader does.
FSIG-03.strengthening: Choose sizes so the record COUNT is unchanged and only content is corrupted (e.g. 100, 300, 700 bytes: 100 stale + 300 still fits one record), and assert content equality of entry 2 as a boolean after reading it back; the extra-entry tell disappears, the reader's skip/read logic becomes an equally weighted suspect, and the writer is no longer implicated by 'an entry appeared'.

FSIG-04.why: The trigger's distinguishing feature is a chunked READ, and Claude greps exactly the methods the test calls, so it reaches TarArchiveInputStream.read in one or two calls and reads it whole (a 'grep -n read( -A70' style call). Inside that one method the correct idiom 'System.arraycopy(rec, sz, readBuf, 0, recLen - sz)' sits 27 lines below the mutated 'System.arraycopy(readBuf, 0, newBuf, 0, newLen)', and the immediately preceding line copies readBuf from offset 0 to the output; a model that simulates two consecutive reads (both models simulate with concrete values) sees the remainder must start at sz. The writer's write() is symmetric but nothing in the test exercises it unusually, and it produces a correct archive that the model can reason about. Decoys with checkable arithmetic at the same depth were ranked 4-6 in the hypothesis-ambiguity experiment, and this is the same situation. The boolean-only assertion costs Claude nothing it had.
FSIG-04.what_would_rescue_the_model: Reading read() end to end and comparing the two remainder copies; mentally running read #2 and read #3 with 100-byte chunks against a 512-byte record.
FSIG-04.strengthening: Mutate the OTHER remainder copy instead: change 'System.arraycopy(rec, sz, readBuf, 0, recLen - sz)' to 'System.arraycopy(rec, 0, readBuf, 0, recLen - sz)'; the buggy line then matches the shape of the correct 'System.arraycopy(rec, 0, buf, offset, sz)' four lines above it, removing the within-method contrast that rescues the model while keeping the identical chunked-read symptom.

FSIG-05.why: Verified: the reused child keeps _index 0 and the generator emits {"a":{"x":1},"b":{,"y":2}}. For Claude (no failure text) the test is 'generate then parse', and Claude knows the generator produced the document, so it follows writeStartObject -> createChildObjectContext -> reset in about three greps. JsonWriteContext is 178 lines; the constructor that sets _index = -1 is ten lines above reset(), and writeFieldName's '_index < 0 ? AS_IS : AFTER_COMMA' is in the same file, so the ordinary '-A' context on any of these greps exposes the missing line by contrast with the constructor. Ownership (reset vs createChildObjectContext) is the residual risk, but createChildObjectContext's explicit 'return ctxt.reset(TYPE_OBJECT)' states the contract that reset reinitialises, and the observed models honour stated contracts. GPT runs the test, gets column 20, and can map it to the first field of the second sibling, which implicates the reuse path directly.
FSIG-05.what_would_rescue_the_model: Seeing the constructor's _index = -1 next to reset()'s three assignments, or reading writeFieldName's _index test before reset(); GPT additionally by computing the column-20 position in the generated string.
FSIG-05.strengthening: Generate through createGenerator(OutputStream) so the writer side is UTF8JsonGenerator (a second, larger generator implementation that also delegates to JsonWriteContext, widening the writer-side candidate set), and nest the sibling objects at depth 3 behind 30+ preceding fields so the parser's column number no longer pinpoints the second sibling for the model that runs the test.

FSIG-06.why: The definer-attribution lever from PIE-03 required the definer to be ON the executed path and able to absorb the fix; here updateBounds() is never executed in the failing scenario and add() computes the incremental cache correctly, so simulating the test refutes both decoys the way the second assertion refuted the same-depth arithmetic decoys. The test calls add three times then remove, and Claude greps the methods named in the test; remove()'s condition lists three of the four cached extremes with the min-incl-stddev pair present and the max-incl-stddev pair absent, an asymmetry a model that knows getRangeBounds(true) reads maximumRangeValueIncStdDev will count. A grep for maximumRangeValueIncStdDev also returns no hit inside remove(), which is the same absent-line tell that makes missing-reset bugs findable. The boolean assertion removes nothing Claude had, and GPT's expected/actual would only help it further.
FSIG-06.what_would_rescue_the_model: Simulating add/add/add/remove and asking why updateBounds was not called; enumerating the four cache pairs from updateBounds against the three in remove()'s condition.
FSIG-06.strengthening: Reach the stale value through a consumer in another class that the test names instead of getRangeBounds, e.g. DatasetUtilities.findRangeBounds(dataset, true) or a StatisticalBarRenderer.findRangeBounds path, so the failing test source mentions add/remove only in passing and the lexical and call-graph pull goes to DatasetUtilities/renderer code, lengthening the path back to remove()'s condition.

FSIG-07.why: This is the recipe both models have already beaten, doubled: the gold formula '(index + at) * width' is the exact bug shape GPT 5/5 and Claude 3/3 diagnosed as 'treats a bit offset as a word index' from the formula alone, and here the correct mirror 'index * width + at' sits in the SAME class (NumberUtils.overlay), giving a side-by-side contrast the original never offered. Coarse signal costs Claude nothing (it had none), and the parameter row {0,16,1} is in the test source, so it simulates dstPos=16 and gets shift 512 masked to 0 for the inverse chain. Twelve hops raise Claude's call count from about 6 to about 12 and GPT's from about 30 to more, but more hops have never raised the error rate. Residual risk is a mid-tier model reading the forward chain, finding nothing, and ranking a facade or the mirror hop by fatigue.
FSIG-07.what_would_rescue_the_model: Reading both deepest hops in NumberUtils and seeing the asymmetry; simulating the [2] parameter case; noticing longToIntArray tests are the ones rerouted.
FSIG-07.strengthening: Put the inverse chain's deepest hop in a different class from overlay (e.g. org.apache.commons.lang3.math.IEEE754rUtils or Fraction) so no same-file mirror exists, and make the parameterized failure the ONLY failing case by choosing dstPos values where the forward and inverse formulas coincide for every other row, so the model cannot triangulate from which rows pass.

FSIG-08.why: Verified by simulation: the buggy contract leaves {4..10,18,19,20}, mean 10.6. The delayed cache-style failure and the on-path definer of startIndex (addElementRolling) are real levers, and expand()'s legitimate copy-from-0 immediately above contract() gives the buggy idiom cover. But contract() is five lines and the next statement is 'startIndex = 0' under a comment 'Reset the start index to zero'; a model that reads it (Claude reaches addElementRolling in two greps and 'if (shouldContract()) contract();' is right there) has to ask why the start index is reset if the copy did not relocate from it, and expand() visibly does NOT reset startIndex, so the contrast cuts the other way once both are read. GPT runs the test, gets 15.5 vs 10.6, and can compute that 10.6 is the mean of stale early values plus the last three, which points at a resize retaining old elements. Weak Claude may stop at addElementRolling's index arithmetic without opening contract().
FSIG-08.what_would_rescue_the_model: Opening contract() and pairing 'arraycopy(internalArray, 0, ...)' with the following 'startIndex = 0'; comparing with expand(), which copies from 0 but leaves startIndex alone; GPT by decoding 10.6 as a stale-window mean.
FSIG-08.strengthening: Reach contract() through an on-path DEFINER of startIndex: have the test call stats.setWindowSize(5) after the 20 adds so discardFrontElements -> discardExtremeElements (which visibly advances startIndex and decrements numElements) runs immediately before shouldContract()/contract(); the model then has a method that manipulates startIndex directly on the executed path to blame, matching the PIE-03 pattern of attributing to the definer of the wrong-looking quantity.

DEPTH-01.why: Strongest of the set because the decoy is REAL code that trips the models' observed lever. In CHART-PIE-03 (10/10 wrong) both models resolved a multi-site sign ambiguity by blaming the hop whose body contradicts its own name; roundUnscaled's `case ROUND_CEILING: if (sign == -1) floor(...)` and the mirrored FLOOR case read as two consistently inverted branches, which reinforces rather than weakens the story, and the trace with the buggy factor reproduces the observed -1.24 exactly (unscaled=-123.4568, sign=-1 -> floor). Claude ranks the deepest arithmetic hop first by default (CONVERSION-LONG 9/9: overlay rank 1) and stops 0-1 calls after a satisfying culprit. Crucially, even a model that escapes the roundUnscaled trap must still choose among H2 (factor lacks `* sign`), H3 (`x * factor` 'should be abs'), and H4 (`/ factor` 'should restore sign') with no local contract distinguishing them unless it recalls the canonical Precision.round(float) body; this three-way ownership split depresses gold@1 further. Facade, H1 and H2 all read as complete natural code; nothing in the chain 'defines' a wrong-looking quantity except roundUnscaled's sign branches.
DEPTH-01.what_would_rescue_the_model: (a) Reading roundUnscaled's javadoc ('Rounds the given non-negative value'; '@param sign Sign of the original, scaled value') which sits 11 lines above the declaration; Opus DID read the leaf with n-15 in CONVERSION-LONG run-001 and GPT's sed slabs always include it. (b) Checking a second rounding mode from the visible test source: `round(-x, 2, ROUND_DOWN)` expects -1.23 but a signed unscaled gives floor(-123.45)=-124 with no sign branch to flip, which refutes the 'invert the branches' hypothesis and forces 'unscaled must be a magnitude'. (c) Recall of the canonical Commons Math body `factor = pow(10, scale) * sign` (Opus more likely). (d) Noticing decimalFactor receives `sign` and merely forwards it.
DEPTH-01.strengthening: Replace the trigger with a narrow new test (e.g. PrecisionTest#testRoundFloatNegativeDirected) asserting only CEILING and FLOOR on negative inputs (-1.23f and -1.24f for -1.2345f), so the visible test source contains no ROUND_DOWN / HALF_* negative case that refutes the 'flip the sign branches in roundUnscaled' hypothesis; a branch flip then satisfies everything the model can see and Claude, which never runs tests, has nothing to contradict it. Keep the non-negative contract only in roundUnscaled's javadoc (above the declaration).

DEPTH-02.why: The bit-identical PIE-03 signature (87.5 vs 112.5) and the 10/10 record on this geometry are real evidence, and with `inner - outer` in drift and `- deltaX` in shift the model now has TWO downstream bodies that read against their names, so the PIE-03 lever has satisfying targets. But the reversal changes the arithmetic in a way the models' observed method detects: in PIE-03 a by-name/value trace reproduced the WRONG value and the model only had to pick a site; here a by-name trace (inner = unexploded point (100,200), outer = exploded (50,200), dx=+50, x = 100 - 12.5) yields the EXPECTED 87.5, so any model that computes (Claude did: 'point1=(100,200) and point2=(50,200), so dx=+50 ... 112.5') hits a contradiction and must bind actual arguments, at which point `drift(unexploded, explodePercent, rimPoint, anchor)` against `(Point2D inner, Point2D outer)` exposes the swap; `rimPoint` landing in `inner` is also a lexical cue. Weak Claude in ADV-DEPTH-01 chased the origin over the convenient fix site. Net: roughly a coin flip, better for weak models that pattern-match than for Opus which traces.
DEPTH-02.what_would_rescue_the_model: Computing the chain by parameter semantics and getting the test's expected value (forces a binding check); the `rimPoint`->`inner` name mismatch in adjacent grep outputs; drift's @param javadoc (GPT reads it via sed; Claude's hardened PIE-03 run-001 also read javadocs post-hoc); noticing that drift and shift are mutually consistent (inward vector then subtract = outward) so neither needs a flip.
DEPTH-02.strengthening: Hide the swap inside a positional call to a real JDK constructor and revive the PIE-03 bait: rim builds `Line2D bisector = new Line2D.Double(rimPoint, anchor)` (gold; correct is `(anchor, rimPoint)`), drift takes `Line2D bisector` with javadoc 'P1 on the unexploded ring, P2 on the exploded ring' and computes `dx = bisector.getX1() - bisector.getX2()`. drift's `P1 - P2` then reads exactly like PIE-03's `point1 - point2` (the proven decoy), the swap is a neutral (p1,p2) constructor argument order two hops above, and the locals should be renamed to neutral `p1`/`p2` so no name hints at ring membership.

DEPTH-03.why: Direct negative evidence exists: adversarial-break-v1 ADV-DEPTH-01 is the same mechanism (mask dropped upstream in the same chain, same trigger, same signature -55035966660880) with overlay's javadoc even PROMISING the mask, and every completed weak-Claude run ranked the upstream origin first (Sonnet 4.6 run-001 top3 widen/combine/overlay; Haiku 4.5 run-001 widen first). Sonnet's evidence chain enumerated both repair sites ('overlay could also mask the word by field before shifting, but the root cause is widen's sign extension') and chose the origin. DEPTH-03's refinement, removing the definition `words[i] = run[i]` so the widening is implicit in the call argument, does raise difficulty because there is no line to point at, but the models that saw 0xFFFF in the high half went hunting for the int->long boundary (Haiku compiled a SignExtensionTest.java to confirm), and combine(int[] words) -> overlay(long word) is the only such boundary in the chain. overlay's javadoc ('already reduced to field') is visible to GPT (sed), Sonnet (sed) and to Opus when it reads the leaf with n-15 as it did in CONVERSION-LONG run-001, and it hands ownership to combine. Opus's default 'lowest-level placement operation' prior and overlay having `field` in hand keep this near a coin flip rather than a win.
DEPTH-03.what_would_rescue_the_model: Identifying sign extension from the actual value (0xFFFFCDF1F0C1DEF0) and then searching for the int->long boundary, which is uniquely combine's call argument; overlay's '@param word ... already reduced to {@code field}' contract; the memorised original `(0xffffffffL & src[i + srcPos])` idiom which lives at the widening site, not the shift; weak Claude's habit of compiling probe programs that print each hop's value.
DEPTH-03.strengthening: Make the boundary look deliberately handled so the hunt stops at combine and moves to the leaf: write the call as `NumberUtils.overlay(total, (long) words[i], i, at, width, field)`. An explicit cast reads as 'conversion taken care of' (and is not a definition the definer heuristic can anchor on) while `(long) int` still sign-extends; overlay's unmasked `word << shift` then becomes the only place that looks deficient. Alternatively/additionally give combine a javadoc that honestly describes widening as its job ('Widens each int word and places it...') so its body reads as textbook for its name.

DEPTH-04.why: The attack's premise that the models do not check positional alignment is untested, and the specific mismatch here is textually salient: the call reads `dosFields(day, month, dosYear, ...)` while the signature one grep later reads `dosFields(int month, int day, int year, ...)`, i.e. the same two identifiers in swapped order, which is the kind of contradiction the models' observed lever (body vs own contract) picks up. GPT decodes bit fields and does arithmetic verification (CMP-LAYOUT: `print(100+8+8+8+12+12)`, jshell probes); once it knows the symptom is month=4/day=3 it looks for a swap, and dateWord/dosValue are vindicated by the in-file oracle `dosToJavaTime` (`>> 21 & 0x0f` month, `>> 16 & 0x1f` day), the sibling-formula lever cited in nearly every past hit. Claude decodes less readily, which is where the residual probability lives, plus the genuine chance that a model that DOES notice blames dosFields' 'odd' US order rather than the caller. Six same-typed ints across three conventions (day/month, month/day, year/month/day) is real plumbing ambiguity that has never been tested, so this is a legitimate probe rather than a rerun of a beaten attack.
DEPTH-04.what_would_rescue_the_model: Decoding 711207107 vs 713238723 (python3 is available in bash) showing month and day exchanged; the identical identifiers `day, month` vs `month, day` in consecutive tool outputs; `dosToJavaTime` in the same ZipUtil file confirming the packer layout; dosFields' javadoc naming month 1-12 / day 1-31.
DEPTH-04.strengthening: Remove the named locals from the swapped call so the mismatch needs API knowledge rather than reading: have dosStamp take the `Date` (or Calendar) and call `ExtraFieldUtils.dosFields(time.getDate(), time.getMonth() + 1, dosYear, time.getHours(), ...)` into `(int month, int day, ...)`. `getDate()` does not read as 'day' and the `+ 1` on the month reads as 'handled', so the swap is no longer a visible identifier reversal. Keep the assertion on the raw long (as designed) so the failure text does not spell out month/day.

DEPTH-05.why: Weaker than its authors expect because, as designed, nothing downstream reads wrong: pack's parameter names lo/mid/hi are semantically loaded and its body `(hi << 16) | (mid << 8) | lo` is exactly right for those names, so the models' proven lever (blame the body that contradicts its own name) has no target below the gold. Both models know Base64 (encode({1,2,3}) = 'AQID'); GPT will decode 'AwIB' to {3,2,1} and Claude likely recognises the reversal, and the only reversal site is the binding `pack(variant, sb, b0, b1, b2)` against `(int lo, int mid, int hi)`, which is visible in adjacent grep outputs and puts the first byte into the least-significant slot. The residual probability comes from models that skip decoding and rank shift-heavy code by failure vocabulary, and from those that, having noticed, prefer to 'fix' pack's unconventional little-endian parameter order rather than the caller (pack's javadoc documenting lo as least significant makes that the minority reading).
DEPTH-05.what_would_rescue_the_model: Decoding the actual output to {3,2,1}; the loaded names lo/mid/hi making pack self-consistent; pack's @param javadoc; the b0->lo binding being one line from the signature; TextBuffer.sextets being the textbook RFC 4648 split.
DEPTH-05.strengthening: Turn the parameter names into a false friend for the caller: declare `pack(Base64Variant variant, StringBuilder sb, int octet0, int octet1, int octet2)` with javadoc 'octet0 occupies bits 0-7 (least significant) of the 24-bit group, octet2 bits 16-23', body `(octet2 << 16) | (octet1 << 8) | octet0`. The caller's `pack(variant, sb, b0, b1, b2)` now aligns lexically (b0->octet0) while violating the documented bit-position contract, and pack's body reads 'reversed' to anyone who assumes octet0 is the first input byte, handing the PIE-03 lever a decoy. The gold stays defensible because pack's contract is explicit.

DEPTH-06.why: The visible test source refutes the intended decoy without running anything: for the same value 60 it expects TOP=90 (= 10 + 0.2*400, the normal mapping) and LEFT=290 (= 350 - 0.2*300, flipped), so the flip is edge-specific, and the only edge-specific code in the chain is the LEFT/RIGHT branch in AxisSpace.locate, the gold. The `if (inverted) fraction = 1.0 - fraction` decoy never executes for a default NumberAxis (DEFAULT_INVERTED=false, and the test only calls setInverted later), and a compensating edit there would break the TOP assertion the model can read. The definer heuristic here points AT the gold (locate defines min/max per edge). A strong sibling oracle exists in the same repo: `max = area.getMinY(); min = area.getMaxY();` untouched in LogAxis.java:357, ModuloAxis.java:256 and NumberAxis's own java2DToValue, and past hits cited such oracles almost universally; Opus also memorises this JFreeChart idiom. Construction note: the proposed inverted-TOP expectation 130.0 is wrong (max - f*(max-min) = 410 - 80 = 330.0); as written the fixed build fails the test.
DEPTH-06.what_would_rescue_the_model: The TOP/LEFT expected values in the test source; knowing `inverted` is false on the failing call; grep for isLeftOrRight/getMinY revealing three sibling implementations with the flipped assignment; memorised JFreeChart valueToJava2D; hand-computing 50 + 0.2*300 = 110 from the gold's own assignments.
DEPTH-06.strengthening: Remove the edge-specific tell from what the model can see: assert only LEFT (and RIGHT) in the new test, dropping TOP/BOTTOM and the inverted cases, so a global-flip hypothesis at Axis.orient (`if (!inverted) fraction = 1 - fraction`) is a complete compensating edit for the visible assertions; route NumberAxis.java2DToValue through the same chain (or a mirrored one) so the in-file oracle disappears (LogAxis/ModuloAxis remain). Also fix the inverted-TOP expectation to 330.0 if it is kept.

DEPTH-07.why: The inversion is carried by an antonym pair that sits in consecutive tool outputs for Claude (translate's `RangeType.offset(lower, upper, delta, allowZeroCrossing)` then offset's `boolean clampAtZero`) and in one sed slab for GPT. offset's body and javadoc are consistent with its own name (`if (!clampAtZero)` -> plain shift), so the models' PIE-03 lever exonerates offset and the odd one out is the caller, which is the gold. The real `shiftWithNoZeroCrossing` clamp is textbook for its name. Both models have shown they read parameter names as evidence (Claude derived direction from `arc1 = new Arc2D.Double(unexploded, ...)` without javadoc) so an antonym is the easiest swap to catch. The authors themselves rank it weakest; I agree and put it lower.
DEPTH-07.what_would_rescue_the_model: Seeing `allowZeroCrossing` passed into `clampAtZero`; offset's javadoc; the failing case being `true` yet clamped, which with offset's `if (!clampAtZero)` immediately implies the flag arrived inverted; the 2-arg `shift(base, delta)` -> `shift(base, delta, false)` sibling and testShift's `false` cases confirming the polarity convention.
DEPTH-07.strengthening: Replace the antonym with a polarity-opaque contract: `offset(double lower, double upper, double delta, boolean signPreserving)` documented 'if true each bound keeps its sign (is held at zero)'. Passing `allowZeroCrossing` into `signPreserving` then requires reasoning about polarity rather than spotting an antonym, and `if (!signPreserving) return new Range(lower + delta, ...)` reads natural. Alternatively map the flag through a real RangeType constant two hops up (`allowZeroCrossing ? RangeType.FULL : RangeType.POSITIVE`) so the swap lives in a ternary rather than a boolean forward.

CANDOVL-01.why: The bug is a visible copy-paste mismatch (`clone.fillPaintList = (PaintList) this.paintList.clone();`) at AbstractRenderer.java:3181, only 20 lines below the `protected Object clone()` declaration at 3161, so Claude's characteristic `grep -n 'Object clone' -A30 AbstractRenderer.java` window contains it; LLMs catch this kind of mismatch reliably once it is in context. The test name `testEqualsAfterDraw` plus the visible `createBufferedImage` line tells an expert model that render-time auto-population (lookupSeriesPaint -> setSeriesPaint, which both models know from JFreeChart) is what distinguishes this from every existing clone/equals test, which points straight at AbstractRenderer rather than the JFreeChart -> CategoryPlot equals descent the attack relies on. The attack works only when the model commits to reading equals bodies first and exhausts its 6-7 calls there - plausible for a mid-tier model, roughly a coin flip for Opus.
CANDOVL-01.what_would_rescue_the_model: Knowing that autoPopulateSeriesPaint fills paintList during a draw, then one declaration-anchored grep of AbstractRenderer.clone (the -A30 window already includes the buggy line) and noticing the field-name mismatch.
CANDOVL-01.strengthening: Hide the render: perform the one draw inside BarChartTests.setUp() (or a helper) so the shown failing-method source is only `clone = chart.clone(); assertTrue(chart.equals(clone));` with no draw hint; and use the attack's own fallback pair (line chart, `clone.outlineStrokeList = (StrokeList) this.strokeList.clone();` at ~line 3197) which sits 36 lines below the declaration, outside a -A30 window, and whose names contrast less than fillPaint/paint.

CANDOVL-02.why: A write-then-read test makes both models read both sides, and CpioArchiveOutputStream lines 195-242 hold all three writers in one 50-line window: writeNewEntry's `pad(... + entry.getName().length() + 1, 4)` and the `writeBinaryLong(entry.getName().length() + 1, 2, ...)` two lines above the gold make the missing `+ 1` a spot-the-difference, and both models know a CPIO namesize includes the NUL. The `!swapHalfWord` decoy is used symmetrically by long2byteArray and byteArray2long, so it cannot break a round trip - Opus will reason that out. Crucially the CHART-PIE-03 mechanism cuts the wrong way here: the wrong-looking quantity is the pad count, and its definer is the gold itself, so the definer heuristic helps the model. GPT's repository greps for `pad(` surface the writer immediately.
CANDOVL-02.what_would_rescue_the_model: Reading writeOldBinaryEntry once and comparing its pad line with writeNewEntry's or with the namesize it wrote two lines earlier; or recognising the byte-swap decoy is symmetric and irrelevant to a round trip.
CANDOVL-02.strengthening: Drop the content assertion and check only names/count so the observed failure becomes `IOException: Unknown magic [..]` thrown from CpioArchiveInputStream.getNextCPIOEntry on the second header: the reader frames and the magic read via readBinaryLong -> CpioUtil.byteArray2long(!swapHalfWord) put the decoy directly on the failure path and pull attention away from the writer.

CANDOVL-03.why: This is the one attack whose bug is a pure absence inside a private helper while the wrong-looking quantity (`intLen`) is DEFINED and counted in the caller parseNumberText and consumed visibly in ParserBase._parseNumericValue's `len <= 9 / <= 18 / == 10` ladder - exactly the definer-attribution pattern that beat both models in CHART-PIE-03; Claude never splits the two modes (no test runs, no scratch programs) so it cannot even confirm the byte parser is at fault. What keeps it from 'very likely' is that the test name `AcrossBufferBoundaries` and the visible 1500-number construction hand an expert model the mechanism: Opus knows UTF8StreamJsonParser has a split-across-boundary helper (`_parserNumber2`'s javadoc says so) and a grep for loadMore/boundary lands on it; reading it beside ReaderBasedJsonParser.parseNumberText2 exposes that intPartLength is passed in and returned unchanged. GPT-5.6 can additionally isolate the mode with a scratch main.
CANDOVL-03.what_would_rescue_the_model: Grepping 'boundary' or 'loadMore' in UTF8StreamJsonParser, then noticing that _parserNumber2 returns resetInt(negative, intPartLength) without ever incrementing the parameter, ideally after reading the reader sibling's `++intLen` loop.
CANDOVL-03.strengthening: Remove the mechanism hint from the shown source: rename the test (e.g. testLargeIntegerArraySumBothModes) and build the document and expected sum in a test-class helper (`String DOC = buildLongIntArrayDoc(1500)`) so the failing-method text shows neither size nor the word boundary; keep the mode loop on one line as designed.

CANDOVL-04.why: getNorm is a 20-line method the model will read as soon as it looks at BlockRealMatrix's overrides, and `Arrays.fill(colSums, jWidth, BLOCK_SIZE, 0.0)` is a wrong-looking range, not an absence: a reader who asks 'where is the used part of colSums reset between block columns?' catches it, and the wrong quantity (colSums) is defined inside the gold, so the definer heuristic favours the model. Opus also knows Block matrices are 52-blocked, will infer from 55 columns that a second block column is the discriminator, and can grep BlockRealMatrixTest to see getNorm is only tested at 3x3/2x3 while multiply/transpose have testSeveralBlocks - a coverage argument that ranks getNorm first even without spotting the line. The complexity prior toward the 60-line unrolled multiply is real for a mid-tier model that reads multiply/transpose first and runs out of calls; GPT can isolate the implementation with a scratch program.
CANDOVL-04.what_would_rescue_the_model: Reading getNorm and questioning the fill range, or grepping the Block test file for getNorm coverage and noticing it never exercises >52 columns.
CANDOVL-04.strengthening: Delete the `Arrays.fill(colSums, 0, jWidth, 0.0);` line outright instead of changing its range: `new double[BLOCK_SIZE]` is already zeroed so the method reads as clean idiomatic code and the defect becomes an absence (no per-block reset), which the models are demonstrably worse at noticing than a wrong-looking statement.

CANDOVL-05.why: All six new codec methods live in one file (TarUtils) within ~120 lines, so both models will read the encoder/decoder pairs together in 2-3 greps; both know the star/GNU base-256 layout is one marker byte followed by length-1 payload bytes, so `for (int i = 1; i < length - 1; i++)` next to `i = 1` is catchable about half the time, and the bare boolean does not stop them from reasoning per field (uid 2^22 -> UIDLEN 8 -> parseBinaryLong). The sign/two's-complement arithmetic the attack counts on as noise is dead for this trigger - every value is positive - and Opus will discount it. When the bound is not spotted the models do rank the dispatchers (formatLongOctalOrBinaryBytes / parseOctalOrBinary, definers of 'which encoding') first, which is the attack's genuine power, but that is a coin flip rather than a systematic failure.
CANDOVL-05.what_would_rescue_the_model: Decoding the 8-byte uid field by hand (marker + 7 payload bytes) against the decoder loop, or comparing parseBinaryLong's bounds with formatLongBinary's write loop.
CANDOVL-05.strengthening: Put a negative field on the executed path (e.g. setModTime to a negative epoch so modTime goes through the 0xff-marker binary path and its BigInteger negation code) so the `val--; val ^= ...` / `add(-1).not()` sign handling is live, correct and suspicious, while the failing field remains the positive uid; this turns dead decoy code into a real competing hypothesis.

CANDOVL-06.why: The gold is two hops from the test (ZipFile.getInputStream -> `offsetEntry.dataOffset` -> resolveLocalFileHeaderData), exactly the one-hop-per-grep path Claude follows, and the method's own commented-out legacy block at lines 524-527 spells out the correct formula `+ fileNameLen + extraFieldLen` directly above the buggy live line - a diff both models will catch immediately once the method is in context. Both models know the LFH layout, and for wrong STORED bytes the data-offset computation is the first suspect for anyone who knows ZIP. The 'unicode extra fields' vocabulary does flood GPT's repository greps with extra-field plumbing, but that costs it calls, not the answer; it has 20-33 calls and 3-6 verification calls after gold.
CANDOVL-06.what_would_rescue_the_model: Following dataOffset from getInputStream into resolveLocalFileHeaderData and reading the live line against the commented formula or against the extraFieldLen it just readFully'd.
CANDOVL-06.strengthening: Remove the dead commented-out `dataOffsets.put` block (legitimate cleanup) so the correct formula no longer sits above the buggy line; additionally use DEFLATED entries so the symptom is a `java.util.zip.ZipException` from InflaterInputStream inside the ZipFile stream, whose java.util.zip frames steer models toward the writer's deflate/data-descriptor logic and BoundedInputStream.addDummy rather than the offset arithmetic.

CLAUDE-01.why: This is the only mechanism with an 8/8 precedent, and the recorded rationales show WHY it worked: Claude wrote 'drift's Javadoc describes the displacement from the unexploded point to the exploded point... shift simply adds the displacement, which matches its documentation'; GPT-5.6 wrote 'shift ... adds the supplied deltas ... exposing any upstream sign error'. Both blame the hop whose expression deviates from its natural meaning and exonerate the consumer that does what its name says. Here widen reordering the run is the deviating expression and overlay's `index * width + at` is the textbook one. A second observed behaviour compounds this: in Lang run-003 Claude used the untouched sibling `shortArrayToLong` (`shift = i * 16 + dstPos`, no reversal, still present in Conversion.java) as its correctness oracle; under that oracle overlay matches and widen is the odd one out. Claude also never runs the test in Lang (0/6) and submits on the first coherent explanation. Two counter-forces keep this below 'very likely': (1) unlike CHART-PIE-03, where `dx = point1 - point2` was an undocumented slip, the reversal here is endorsed by two javadocs ('most significant first' in widen and combine), which a contract-minded reader (GPT-5.6 reads more; Opus read shift's javadoc explicitly) can take as deliberate, making overlay the hop that ignores its input's documented order; (2) overlay's `count` parameter, used only in a range check, is a tell that the formula was meant to consume it.
CLAUDE-01.what_would_rescue_the_model: Reading the two 'most significant first' javadocs as a deliberate contract that overlay must honour, or asking why overlay takes `count` if the shift ignores it; running the failing test would not help (the swap is already fully explained by simulation, the question is purely attribution).
CLAUDE-01.strengthening: Remove the explicit 'most significant first' endorsement from widen's javadoc (keep it only in combine's @param, which still defends ownership) and write the reversal as an index-juggling loop (`for (int i = run.length - 1, j = 0; i >= 0; i--, j++) words[j] = run[i] & field;`), so widen reproduces the CHART-PIE-03 pattern of an unexplained deviation rather than a documented convention.

CLAUDE-02.why: The favourable facts are real: every prompt shows 'Failure stack trace: (not provided)', Claude ran the test in 0/6 Lang runs, so the 0xFFFF... signature is never shown, and if the suffix is missed Claude's Lang default is exact reverse-depth order (tau 1.0 in 6/6 runs), which converts a miss cleanly into overlay at rank 1. But `0xffffffff` without L on an int->long path is one of the best-known Java pitfalls and Opus flags it on sight, especially primed by the method's own javadoc ('zero-extended to 64 bits'), by test data that is visibly negative (0xCDF1F0C1), and by the sibling `shortArrayToLong` two screens away using `0xffffL &`. The one existing `0xffffffff &` in Conversion.java (line 1197, cast to int) slightly normalises the look, and a mid-tier model that reads once in a 30-line window is more likely to skim past it, hence the gap between the two estimates.
CLAUDE-02.what_would_rescue_the_model: Noticing the literal's type (int & int, then sign-extended), or running the test once and seeing the top 16 bits set.
CLAUDE-02.strengthening: Take the literal off the screen: have compose compute `final int field = -1 >>> (Integer.SIZE - width);` (a real idiom) and pass an int `field`, so unpack's loop is the textbook `words[i] = run[i] & field;` and the sign extension arises from a parameter type two hops up; keep unpack as the gold (its contract is zero-extension; correct body `run[i] & 0xffffffffL`) and drop the 'zero-extended' wording from its javadoc so nothing primes a suffix check.

CLAUDE-03.why: As specified this is the inverse of CHART-PIE-03: the gold's own javadoc ('numericEnd ... checksum included; returns the type-flag byte which immediately follows the checksum') contradicts its body (`+ CHKSUMLEN`), while numericWidth's body matches its doc. Both models' demonstrated rule blames the doc/body mismatch, which lands on the gold. The Compress record adds a second reason: Claude ran the test 3/3, read TarConstants, and summed offsets numerically ('100+8+8+8+12+12=148 ... writeEntryHeader puts linkFlag at offset 156'); here it will compute 164, see CHKSUMLEN added twice, and the addition at the gold is the one its own contract forbids. The real `offset += CHKSUMLEN` still present in parseTarHeader (line 590) is consistent with numericWidth including the checksum, not against it.
CLAUDE-03.what_would_rescue_the_model: Nothing extra is needed; the default path (numeric offset sum plus contract reading) already reaches checksumBoundary.
CLAUDE-03.strengthening: Make the gold's javadoc silent about the checksum ('@param numericEnd the end of the numeric fields') so `+ CHKSUMLEN` reads as textbook and matches its name, and strip the tar-spec justification from numericWidth's javadoc to a bare field list, so the definer becomes the hop that looks unconventional; even then expect roughly 50/50, because 'numeric block includes the octal checksum' is a defensible reading.

CLAUDE-04.why: The hiding premise fails on two of the three observed Lang idioms: `grep -n "widen" -B3 -A30 BitField.java` (run-002) and `grep -n -B3 -A30 "static long widen"` (run-003) print every matching declaration with 30 lines each, so the int[] overload's declaration and loop are on screen; only run-001's `head -1 | cut -d: -f1` idiom hides it, and even `-A30 | head -60` reaches roughly line 55 of the second block. compose declares `final int[] run` while the first overload takes `long[]`, and Opus resolves overloads. CLAUDE-04.what_would_rescue_the_model: Any grep for 'widen' without `head -1`, overload resolution from compose's `int[]` parameter, or a re-read when hops 4-5 are visibly correct.
CLAUDE-04.strengthening: Push the int[] overload's loop past +30 of its own declaration behind Lang-style guards, so a `-A30` on the second declaration shows only guards while the correct first-overload loop primes 'same body'; this defeats the -A30 idioms too, though Opus still tends to re-read a method that has not closed.

CLAUDE-05.why: The artifact is already refuted in the record: in five MATH-HARMONIC trajectories GPT-5.6 submitted `HarmonicFitter.ParameterGuesser::guessAOmega`, received the tool's structured `class_not_found` (distinct from `method_not_found`, so the model learns the class spelling is wrong), and resubmitted `HarmonicFitter$ParameterGuesser::...` on the very next call; 47 catalog-valid `$` predictions exist across runs. The submit tool returns errors with returncode 1 and lets the agent retry, and Opus knows JVM binary names at least as well. The bug itself (`> 0` vs `>= 0` on binarySearch, with ',' sorting to index 0 of ",;") is trivial for both models given the test source. Only a weak model that abandons the nested class after rejection would fall to `StrMatcher::isMatch`.
CLAUDE-05.what_would_rescue_the_model: The `class_not_found` feedback plus binary-name knowledge, which is exactly what rescued GPT-5.6.
CLAUDE-05.strengthening: Put the gold in an anonymous StrMatcher subclass (binary name `StrMatcher$1::isMatch`), which a model cannot derive without counting anonymous classes in the file; verify first that the catalog spells anonymous classes that way and that the scorer accepts it, otherwise the attack has no valid gold key.

CLAUDE-06.why: The wrongness is inherited, not created: the design keeps PlotUtilities.drift's `dx = point1 - point2`, the definer that took rank 1 in 8/8 CHART-PIE-03 runs across both models (gold rank 6 for GPT, 3-6 for Claude), so this is CHART-PIE-03 plus a decoy and drift, not PiePlot::shift, is the expected rank-1. The shadow itself adds little: the call in Plot.nudge is unqualified, so the natural next step is a grep inside Plot.java, which lands on the gold; grep -r in the run workspace does list plot/PiePlot.java before plot/Plot.java (verified, positions 98 vs 103), so the `-A15 | head -20` idiom would show PiePlot.shift first, but Opus knows static methods bind to the declaring class, and since both shift bodies use `+` the sight of two adding shifts reinforces 'the sign convention is upstream' and pushes blame to drift anyway.
CLAUDE-06.what_would_rescue_the_model: Only what would have rescued it in CHART-PIE-03 and did not: treating drift's javadoc as ambiguous and asking which hop's contract the test actually constrains; static-binding knowledge defeats the shadow but not the definer.
CLAUDE-06.strengthening: The shadow only bites if the executed method looks wrong by name while the decoy looks right: give PiePlot.shift the correct sign (`-`) with a real label-drawing caller, so a model that misapplies dynamic dispatch reads a correct shift and has nothing left but drift/nudge; otherwise drop the shadow and put the effort into 07, since 06's marginal value over plain CHART-PIE-03 is near zero.

The padding's own contribution is close to zero for Opus: in every observed truncation Claude followed up when the method had not visibly closed (`ring -A40 | head -90` then `sed -n 885,940p`; `shift -A12` then `sed -n 700,716p` to read the javadoc; Lang n+25 windows), and in CHART-PIE-03 Claude DID see `x + deltaX` and still exonerated shift ('simply adds the displacement, which matches its documentation'), so hiding the `+` removes an exoneration it never needed. CLAUDE-07.what_would_rescue_the_model: Nothing beyond what CHART-PIE-03 already failed to provide; re-reading the unclosed method only restores the CHART-PIE-03 state.

CMB-01.why: The buggy code the model sees is byte-for-byte the code Claude saw in CHART-PIE-TREATMENT-03: drift = p1-p2 under the same 'drift between a point on the unexploded ring and the corresponding point on the exploded ring' javadoc, nudge = dx*explodePercent, shift = x+dx, same ArcProbe test, same expected:<87.5> but was:<112.5>. The only pin Claude sees is the facade guard on step 1 (`grep -n intArrayToLong -A30`), and decoding `lane(dstPos,32) + nInts - 1 > 2` as equivalent to the javadoc's `(nInts-1)*32+dstPos >= 64` only under a 1-based lane is algebra with no observed precedent; ConversionTest-1f has no IllegalArgumentException test for intArrayToLong, so nothing executable enforces it. CMB-03.why: The premise that Claude read writeEntryHeader in 1/3 CMP-LAYOUT-02 runs is wrong: it displayed it in 3/3 (run-001 bundled `writeEntryHeader\|parseTarHeader -A30`, runs 002/003 used `sed -n 480,620p`, covering lines 536-567) and computed 148 -> 156 explicitly, so the `c <= csLast` pin WILL be on screen; the fight is over interpretation. Two cues push back: the method name 'Last' and the inclusive fill loop. TarUtils.typeFlagOffset (H1, passing a Last into an End) is a third plausible blame target, which adds to p_wrong. Expect Opus to split near even, mid-tier Claude to lean to the -1; GPT (which read writeEntryHeader and grepped CHKSUMLEN in both CMP-LAYOUT runs) similar to Opus.
CMB-03.what_would_rescue_the_model: Noticing checksumLast is consumed inclusively (`for (c = csOffset; c <= csLast; ++c)`) in writeEntryHeader, and that typeFlagPosition's javadoc says the flag FOLLOWS the field while its body returns the argument unchanged.

CMB-04.why: The mechanism assumes Claude never displays sibling loops, but Claude's observed helper greps are bare-name with context on ALL hits (`grep -rn "identityWidth" src/main -A12 | head -40`, `grep -n "nudge(" -B3 -A20`, `grep -n "combine" -B3 -A30`); lastScanBound has 11 hits in ArrayUtils.java and even `| head -40` shows the Object[] (1687) and long[] (1798) siblings' `for (int i = bound - 1;` before the int[] gold at 1901, exposing the odd-one-out. GPT's repo-wide `grep -rn lastScanBound -A3` shows all ten call sites. CMB-04.what_would_rescue_the_model: Any context grep on lastScanBound, reading the long[] sibling named in the test, or reasoning that a helper shared by ten overloads is less likely wrong than the one loop that starts AT an exclusive bound (and would throw AIOOBE on lastIndexOf(array, 0, 88)).

CMB-05.why: The search trap is thinner than claimed in this checkout: ReaderBasedJsonParser-1f uses reset(negative, intLen, fractLen, expLen), not resetInt, so `grep -rn resetInt` returns 4 hits (ParserBase.reset, UTF8 parseNumberText, and two inside _parserNumber2), landing on the gold, where `resetInt(negative, _textBuffer.size() - 1)` sits 20 lines from the correct `resetInt(negative, intPartLength)` in the SAME method, a glaring inconsistency that the proposed 'the sign is not a digit' comment advertises. The residual risk is a mid-tier model stopping at ParserBase._parseNumericValue or NumberInput.parseLong with a lexical story, or being unsure whether byte[] input selects the UTF-8 parser.
CMB-05.what_would_rescue_the_model: Grepping `_intLength` or `resetInt` (a 4-hit result), or contrasting the EOF and non-EOF resetInt calls in _parserNumber2; verifying parseLong is correct for len=13 forces the search upstream.
CMB-05.strengthening: Drop the comment; derive the count through a shared, correctly documented ParserBase helper (e.g. `_textLength()` returning `_textBuffer.size()`) that only the UTF-8 EOF branch decrements; refactor ReaderBasedJsonParser's integer exit to call resetInt too so the grep genuinely returns 6+ sites; and feed the number through an InputStream with a small buffer so the model cannot tell statically which resetInt site executed, and use a 19+ digit value so NumberInput.parseBigInteger becomes a second decoy.

CMB-06.why: The override does no offset arithmetic (it only rewrites '\\' to '/' in place; getUnicodeName returns the internal array so it works), while the failure is a copy-offset shift (one CRC byte prepended, last name byte lost) whose cause is a single line `System.arraycopy(buffer, offset + 4, unicodeName, 0, length - 5)` with a literal 4/5 mismatch, and assembleData writes `data[5]` 60 lines above in the same 171-line file. The registry decode is short-circuited by the test's `instanceof UnicodePathExtraField`; Claude reaches super.parseFromLocalFileData in one grep. In CMP-LAYOUT-02 Claude named the class where the offending line lived (ZipArchiveInputStream.flagOffset, not the tar class it started in), so the declaring-class artifact is unlikely for Opus and only modest for a mid-tier model.
CMB-06.what_would_rescue_the_model: Reading the superclass body: the 4 vs 5 asymmetry and assembleData's layout are both visible; the normalisation in the override visibly succeeded in the actual output ('dir/sub'), exonerating it.
CMB-06.strengthening: Give the override real byte-index work that plausibly yields a one-byte shift, e.g. strip a leading '/' from the decoded name (APPNOTE forbids absolute paths) via `System.arraycopy(name, 1, ...)`, so a same-class candidate with visible offset arithmetic exists; and express the gold's copy offset through constants (e.g. `offset + VERSION_LEN + CRC_LEN - 1` vs `length - HEADER_LEN`) so the 4/5 asymmetry is not literal on one line.

CMB-07.why: Omissions are harder to see than wrong expressions, but Claude's observed style (`grep -n startIndex File.java`, one screen) puts contract()'s `compact(...); startIndex = 0;` and expand()'s `compact(...)` with no reset side by side, and the class javadoc states the window invariant `internalArray[startIndex..startIndex+numElements-1]`; Opus is likely to spot the missing line. MathArrays.compact's javadoc ('placed at the beginning') matches its body, so unlike PIE-03 the definer prior has no doc/body mismatch to feed on. Mid-tier Claude and GPT, reasoning from runtime values, may blame addElementRolling (the method that advanced startIndex to 4/5) or compact (copying from start where the old expand copied from 0), which keeps p_wrong non-trivial. Trace verified: after rolling 9, buggy layout is [5,6,7,8,0,0,0,0,9,...] with startIndex 5, contract yields [0,0,0,9,0], getElement(0)=0.0.
CMB-07.what_would_rescue_the_model: Grepping startIndex in ResizableDoubleArray (shows the reset in contract and its absence in expand), or reading the class-level invariant and asking which method relocated the window without moving its origin.
CMB-07.strengthening: Remove the side-by-side template: keep contract()'s original arraycopy + reset (so compact has a single caller and no 'compact then reset' pattern appears elsewhere), or route both through a private relocate(newSize) that contract resets after and expand does not, so `grep startIndex` shows only contract's reset and the model must infer that expand's relocation also moves the origin; note this raises fix-location ambiguity (relocate becomes a defensible repair site).

RANKING METHOD. Expected Acc@1 reduction is taken as the critic's p_wrong_top1 (averaged over weak Claude and Opus, Opus as tie-break), preferring the critic wherever it disagrees with the designer; the baseline is ~0.95-1.0 so reduction is essentially p_wrong. The top of the list is entirely the one mechanism with measured double failure (CHART-PIE-03: the model blames the method that DEFINES the wrong-looking quantity): CMB-01 (0.88/0.85), CLAUDE-07 (0.90/0.85) and CLAUDE-06 (0.85/0.80) inherit that number from the PIE-03 base almost unchanged (the critic judges the padding and the static-hiding shadow near-zero marginal), CTX-06 (0.85/0.78) is the doc-hygiene control on the same base, CTX-01 (0.88/0.78) is the only Lang design where the depth prior and the definer heuristic point at the same wrong hop, and OWN-01/LEX-01 are re-hostings of the definer split. The search-space family (SSN) and the pure lexical family (LEX-05/06/08) sit at the bottom because every measured run computes the gold's arithmetic and follows one symbol per grep without losing the path; the critic found construction defects or side-by-side oracles in SSN-02/03/04/06/08 and CMB-04/05/06.

TOP-5 SELECTION. Ownership/attribution: CMB-01 rather than CLAUDE-06/07 because it changes what the model sees (non-terminal gold, pure definer, correct textbook terminal) while keeping the byte-identical PIE-03 failure, and the unit-test pin makes the gold uniquely defensible; Chart is used because the patch and trigger already exist there. Deepest-stage prior: CTX-01 on Lang (the strongest non-PIE design, with the critic's field-naming strengthening and the BitField.setValue pin that makes compose the unique all-green fix). Lexical/witness: LEX-01 on Lang, the faithful Lang instance of PIE-03 with the critic's utc/local identifiers and single-line leaf. Candidate overload: CANDOVL-03 on JacksonCore (critic 'likely', 0.70/0.55; a real bug class, one deleted line, both parsers executed in one loop; I simulated the 4000-byte refills to fix the exact failure text 619083340700919 vs 617267060016054 and applied the critic's hide-the-mechanism strengthening). Symbol-directed search is the forced pick: no SSN idea is 'likely' for Opus, so I chose the one the critic could make buildable and strongest, SSN-01 with its verified strengthening (CANONICALIZE_FIELD_NAMES disabled makes constructParser return ReaderBasedJsonParser for UTF-8 bytes, so every surface cue points at the wrong twin), with an honest expected Acc@1 of ~0.40 weak / ~0.50 Opus. Combinations were preferred where buildable: CMB-01 is itself a three-lever combination (definer + non-terminal gold + correct terminal witness + pin), CTX-01 combines the depth prior with a definer decoy and an off-chain contractual pin, and LEX-01 combines the definer split with the Rule-list dispatch of FastDatePrinter (12 appendTo implementations reached through a List<Rule> field) so it also taxes symbol-directed navigation.
